Canadian War Memorials

subtopic: CANADIAN WAR MEMORIALS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN WAR MEMORIALS
subsubtopic: APPRECIATION OF SERVICES OF CANADIAN BATTLEFIELDS MEMORIALS COMMISSION AND DESIGNER OF VIMY MEMORIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the
great war, parliament felt it desirable and fitting that the service and sacrifice of Canada's forces in the war should be commemorated by the erection of appropriate memorials on the fields of battle. With this end in view, the government established, by an order in council of September 2, 1920, the Canadian Battlefields Memorials Commission, consisting of the following members:
Major-General the Hon. S. C. Mewburn.
Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux.
Lt. General Sir R. E. W. Turner.
Lt. Col. R. W. Leonard.
Hon. J. G. Turriff
General Mewburn was designated chairman of the commission, and Colonel H. C. Osborne was appointed secretary. To this body, the task was entrusted of clearing war-torn ground, of planting trees and beds of flowers, of selecting the designs for the different memorials, and, generally, of supervising their construction. For more than a decade and a half the commission has carried on its labours with public-spirited enterprise. Under its auspices eight memorials, comprising the entire group as contemplated at the outset, have been brought to completion. Of these, three are located in Belgium-Passchendaele, St. Julien and "Hill 62," or, as it became known, "Sanctuary Wood." The other five are located in France, at Dury, Bourlon Wood, Courcelette, Le Quesnel, and at Vimy Ridge. In addition, plaques have been placed in the City Hall at Mons and St. Nazaire.
Only three members of the commission, General Mewburn, Hon. Senator Lemieux, and General Richard Turner, together with Colonel Osborne, the secretary, lived to see the completion of all the memorials. Since that time Senator Lemieux has also passed away.
To those who have been privileged to view the memorials, no word of explanation will be required with respect to the resolution now before the house. The members of the commission, serving entirely without remuneration, gave unstintingly of their time and energies to a task which called for the most careful and patient effort. It will be agreed, I believe, that their endeavours merit the recognition of parliament.
Of exceptional significance is the great memorial on Vimy Ridge, of which Mr. Walter S. Allward, of Toronto, is the designer and architect.
Hon. members who were in the house in 1923 will recall a resolution which was passed during the session of that year-a resolution which I had the honour of introducing- expressing the gratitude of the Canadian parliament to the French republic for the gift of 250 acres of land on Vimy Ridge. This gracious act on the part of France ensured that the monument, which Canada proposed to erect on that historic site, might stand on Canadian soil.
The efforts of the Canadian Legion, over a period of two years, in organizing the visit of eight thousand pilgrims to Vimy Ridge for the unveiling of the memorial on July 26, 1936, and the ceremonies incidental thereto, will still be present to the minds of hon. members, and will long be remembered by the Canadian people.
The Vimy memorial fulfils a twofold purpose. It commemorates the valour of our countrymen throughout the long years of the war, and the sacrifice of those who gave their lives in the conflict. It constitutes, in particular, a memorial of the heroic endeavours of the Canadian troops, and of their British and French brothers-in-arms, who fought upon the ridge at Vimy. On the monument are inscribed the names of Canadian soldiers who lie in unknown graves in France.	*
The monument at Vimy has been described as. perhaps, the most beautiful and striking of the memorials of the great war. Mr. Allward has given unsparingly of his artistic genius to interpret and commemorate the spirit and ideals of those who bore arms for Canada in the war. In the memorial he has achieved for the dominion, as for himself, a place of high distinction in the realm of sculpture. Not only has he given to the world a great work of art; he has caught, in an impressive manner, and preserved for our own and succeeding generations, the true significance of Canada's participation in the war. It is most appropriate, therefore, that an expression should be given by the parliament of Canada of its appreciation of Mr. Allward's services, an appreciation which will be shared by the people of Canada generally.
Accordingly, I desire to move, seconded by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett):
That this house desires to record its thanks to the members of the Canadian Battlefields Memorials Commission, who served without remuneration over a period of years, and whose endeavours ensured the erection in France and Belgium of appropriate memorials of the valour and sacrifice of Canada's forces in the great war;
And, that this house desires particularly to express its appreciation of the services of Mr. Walter S. Allward, who, as the designer and
Canadian War Memorials

architect of the memorial at Yimy, has given to the world, a work of art of outstanding beauty and character. Through the years to come the Vimy memorial will remain the symbol of Canada's efforts in the war, and its tribute to those who, on the field of battle, sought to preserve the free institutions of mankind.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADIAN WAR MEMORIALS
subsubtopic: APPRECIATION OF SERVICES OF CANADIAN BATTLEFIELDS MEMORIALS COMMISSION AND DESIGNER OF VIMY MEMORIAL
speechtext:
I regard it, Mr. Speaker, as a great privilege to associate myself with the right hon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the motion that you have just read. I do not propose to do more than state my entire agreement with the sentiments that have been so eloquently expressed by the Prime Minister, because at this time it would be out of place to make any extended observations.
The truth is that honouring the memory of the dead is a matter of very great importance. One of our own great Canadian statesmen, Joseph Howe, in stanzas which I think will live as long as his memory is preserved, has indicated why we should remember the glorious dead. To do so fittingly when our beloved dead rest in far distant lands was an extremely difficult task. When the Canadian Battlefields Memorials Commission was set up they cooperated closely with the British commission headed by General Sir Fabian Ware; and anyone who has visited the battlefields will agree, I think, that the work done has been magnificently conceived and certainly executed in a manner worthy of the highest praise.
Rich and poor, high and low, whatever may have been their place in civil life, find exactly the same memorial in these great cemeteries in France and Flanders. It is fitting that it should be so, because these crosses not only commemorate the valour of our immortal dead but tell the tale of sacrifice forever associated with the cross. I cannot do more than express deep regret that there remain but two, if my memory serves me rightly, of the original members of that commission which was appointed only a few years ago. It is a singular commentary on the brevity of human life.
The conception of this great memorial at Vimy Ridge was that of Mr. Allward of Toronto. The competition, I believe, was open to the world. The problem was how to interpret in stone the genius of a people and to commemorate at once the valour of brave men who gave their lives as a sacrifice for their country. I think it can be said of this memorial that it does interpret the genius of the Canadian people, and every Canadian who looks upon it will be filled with justifiable pride. Let us hope that in future years Canadians of those days will look upon that ridge and read the names of the men who

perished and were buried in nameless graves, but marked for all time on the base of that great monument.
War is a hateful thing, and yet I sometimes feel that however hateful we may think it the fact remains that it has developed those great qualities in men of which we are so proud and of which we speak so often in praise and in recognition of their bravery, their courage, and their sacrifice. All these high qualities are exemplified in war, and the horrors of war. I repeat, I sometimes wonder why it is that in no field of history do we find such evidence of the great qualities of mankind as we find in the tales of their heroism, devotion and sacrifice in time of war, whether it be the Spartans at Thermopylae, or those who died on Vimy Ridge. Yet in our great memorial we have a magnificent work of art, some compensation for the disfiguring results of war.
So I regard it as a privilege to join with the Prime Minister in commending the efforts of the Canadian Battlefields Memorials Commission and in congratulating them upon the splendid service they have rendered to this country, and upon the fitting character and beauty of the memorials they have builded in various parts of France and Flanders, and that future generations may know that this Canadian parliament had a proper realization also of the splendid work done by Mr. Allward, sculptor and artist, in so fittingly interpreting the loyalty, courage and devotion of those who died on Vimy Ridge that we might live.
Mr. J. II. BLACKMORE (Lethbridge): There are before the minds of men to-day several things of priceless value. Perhaps the first of these is democracy. Following that are peace, prosperity and virtue. In order to achieve in the highest degree, and to preserve for the generations yet to come, these precious things, there are in my opinion two great necessities. The first of these is the unity and greatness of the British Empire. The second is the unity and greatness of Canada as part of that empire. The men whose memory we to-day are holding in reverence gave freely for democracy, peace, prosperity and virtue, for the unity and greatness of the British Empire, and for the unity and greatness of Canada. It has been truthfully said, "They served till death. Why not we "?
I have always been thrilled by the words which I understand have been placed on a great memorial to them. With those words I should like to close:
Their name liveth for evermore.

Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
I have a very strong opinion about this matter, and I congratulate the Minister of Justice upon having withdrawn the resolution. I hold the view, which I have expressed in this house frequently, that any member of the legal profession appointed to the bench is assumed to be an expert in law, that it is one of the implied conditions of his appointment that his fitness shall be a continuing fitness, and if for physical or other reasons he is no longer able to maintain his fitness as an expert he should retire. The Judges Act provides that he may retire and receive financial consideration as therein provided. During my term of office we introduced a measure, providing for the retirement of judges who had attained the age of seventy-five years or more, but it was defeated in the

senate. Subsequently I was approached and told that if I so desired certain members of the bench would retire if we would enact legislation providing them with their full salaries. I declined to entertain the proposal, which was submitted to me by members of the profession, some of whom I think felt that they might be likely successors to the positions thus vacated. I took the view, which I still hold, that that was a very improper proposal. I took the view that for the judges of this country to suggest to the government of the day that if they were given their full pay they would retire and make way for someone else was something so scandalous as not to be entertained by any self-respecting government in Canada. I took that view then and I still hold it very strongly, and I congratulate the minister upon not having yielded to that sort of proposal. I was going to call it a threat, but it is worse than that. It is worse than a suggestion. It is-

The origin of the inquiry, the report of which covers some 259 pages, is set out at page 11 of the report. I quote:
The origin of the inquiry is to be found in a report of a special committee of the House of Commons concurred in by the house on June 17, 1936. This report, after dealing with tlie matters which had been specifically referred to the committee, concluded with the following recommendation:
"The committee further gave general consideration to the whole problem of the production and marketing of Canadian wheat and other facts pertaining to the wheat problem. Because of the gravity of this problem, and because your committee has neither the time nor the facilities to make a comprehensive survey of the situation, we recommend the appointment by the government of a royal commission to make a complete survey of the production, grading and distribution of Canadian grain, including the methods of marketing."

And then under paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) are set out the various methods of marketing. I claim that that is not the real origin of the commission. The final report of the special committee, which was tabled on June 11, 1936, a day or two before the close of the session, is a short one, and sets out the names of the witnesses who were heard. We find there were only three, namely Mr. Darby, Mr. Fowler and Mr. Murray. The order of reference of the special committee was to inquire into Mr. Murray's action on December 13, 1935, to see whether or not the charge that he had protected shorts was correct. The second paragraph of the report is in these words:
While there was a short interest in the Winnipeg wheat market in December of 1935, no evidence was produced that would warrant the conclusion that speculative short interests were protected by the board in that month. As the committee finds it impracticable to obtain conclusive evidence on this point, we recommend that this matter be referred for further investigation to the royal commission, the appointment of which is recommended in this report.
There was the origin of the commission- because the committee could not agree. When we heard the evidence of Messrs. Darby, Fowler and Murray, certain members of the committee asked that further witnesses be produced. We were refused. We asked that certain documents be produced, and were refused. It was then in a meeting in camera that the question of the general marketing of grain was considered. No witnesses were heard with respect to that matter, and the question of coarse grains came before the committee only through general discussion. It was decided that at some future time towards the end of the sittings of the committee there might be a discussion of that question, but that discussion was never had.
For these reasons I claim that the committee did not discuss or give any general consideration to the marketing of wheat or wheat products, other than in a meeting in camera. I must point out, however, that that meeting in camera was held after the committee had decided that we were to refer the matter to the royal commission. That is the first order of reference. I have the order of reference before me, but it is not necessary to read it to the committee. I have the statement here which was made by myself with respect to certain documents in the form of offers and acceptances that I had asked to have produced. Request was made also for the names of certain witnesses, but these were all refused when the committee was meeting in camera.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
There have been seventeen grain inquiries during the last thirty odd years, the last four being the most important. On May 1, 1923, a royal commission was appointed headed by Mr. Justice Turgeon, two other gentlemen being associated with him. This commission took evidence in 1924 and reported in January, 1925. They took nearly two years to make their investigation. Then the Stamp commission was appointed by order in council dated April 10, 1931, and reported nineteen days later on April 29. I might say that Sir Josiah Stamp acted without remuneration and this inquiry was carried on at very little cost. I have his report before me.
Then the present Turgeon commission was appointed. It was decided on May 4 that it should be set up and the commission was appointed by order in council dated June 17, 1936. Evidence was taken in 1937 and the report was made more than two years after the commission was appointed. I claim that the cost of this commission was an unnecessary and useless expenditure. The review of the period prior to 1930 set out in this report is similar to the review contained in the report of the Turgeon commission which sat from 1923 to 1925, and the review of the Stamp commission. These summaries are all very similar, and all that was necessary to be done was to review the period since 1930, when the pools began to find themselves in more or less difficulty. In 1929 and 1930 the. provincial governments were called upon to implement certain guarantees which they had made. They could not do this, and the federal government was brought into the picture. They took over the carry-over, and then finally in 1932 Mr. McFarland was called upon to carry on what were generally spoken of as stabilization operations. These operations resulted in an increase in the price of cash wheat from 42 cents, which was the lowest in many years, to 86 cents.
This present report gives credit to Mr. McFarland for the service that he rendered to the country and to western Canada in particular. The report states distinctly that these stabilization operations meant a great deal to the farmers of western Canada and that they received considerably more for their wheat than they would have received if the operations had not been carried out. That was something that we all knew in 1935 when a committee was appointed to consider the wheat board act. Mr. Mclvor appeared before the committee and he was asked the results up to that time of the operations carried out by Mr. McFarland. He told the committee that the farmers of western Canada had been able to sell 1,700,060.000
bushels of wheat during the four year period at a price that he considered to be ten cents a bushel more than they would have received if these operations had not been carried on
This report sets out to the people of Canada the real service that Mr. McFarland rendered. I ask hon. members who were members of the house from 1930 to 1935 to recall the many occasions upon which the Hon. Mr. Ralston, who was seated in this immediate vicinity, attacked the government and Mr. McFarland. The government was charged with providing Mr. McFarland with funds to speculate and gamble in the wheat market. Let me remind hon. members that Mr. McFarland had to go on the market day after day to buy millions of bushels of wheat in order to maintain the price. He did this at a time when he knew the big interests were making raids on the market. On July 21, 1933. he was forced to buy
15,000,000 bushels of wheat. Compare what Mr. McFarland was up against with the action taken by Mr. Murray. On December, 13, 1935, 22,000,000 bushels of cash and option wheat were sold when it was known that prices were likely to increase. During July, 1937, Mr. Murray sold 62,000,000 bushels of wheat, not more than half of which went into export.
Following the change in government in 1935 there was a change in the personnel of the wheat board. Mr. McFarland and one of his associates were let out. Mr. Mclvor was retained, and Mr. Murray was appointed chairman. From the very outset of their appointment this board started to pursue what is commonly spoken of as a fire-sale policy. Marketing conditions in other parts of the world at that time indicated that there would be an increase in price in the month of December, yet, as I said a moment ago, on December 13 that board, under the chairmanship of Mr. Murray, sold 22.000,000 bushels of wheat. Apparently that sale was made under an agreement that had been made on December 11 with a committee of the grain exchange.
Early in 1936 charges were made in the house in connection with that transaction. It was stated that a considerable part of that sale had been made for the purpose of protecting the short interests. It is stated on page 205 of this report that in 1935, when Mr. Murray took over from the McFarland board, there was a total of 177,682,000 bushels in short options. From the commencement of the appointment of the new board Mr. Murray carried on his fire-sale policy, which led to certain charges being made in this house. The main reason for those charges

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
was an article that appeared in a Wall Street journal. I have in my hand a copy of that article, but I do not propose to read it all. It refers to the transaction of December 13, to this extraordinary action on the part of the wheat board. It says:
The Canadian grain board showed its cooperation with exporters, particularly the small ones that had made definite price contracts over night, by allowing them to take in their hedges at one-qnarter cent over the market's close. Had this not been done, the small shippers would have been in a plight, for Winnipeg wheat futures opened up the permissible three cents limit on the following day. Thus exporters who had sold wheat overnight would have been hard pressed to cover their hedges.
Then comes this important paragraph:
As yet no Canadian government, irrespective of its political complexion, has recognized any obligation to succor the grain trading interests. The action of the Murray board, accordingly, constitutes an interesting precedent which is scheduled to be the subject of an important airing at the session to come.
I therefore claim that the leader of the opposition and myself were justified in making the charges that we did on the thirteenth of February, I think it was, and which resulted in a committee being set up. I have already referred to the order of reference to that committee. Mr. Murray was called before this committee and examined, and finally the committee, not being able to find conclusive evidence in either direction as to whether he had or had not taken certain measures, decided to refer the matter to a royal commission.
I want now to refer to some of the evidence given by Mr. Murray before the commission, and to show that from the very first, after he accepted the chairmanship of the board, he pursued a dictatorship policy not only in the selling of wheat, where he apparently did just as he pleased, but in other matters as well. I quote from page 9191 of the evidence, where Mr. Murray was being examined by Mr. MacPherson, counsel for the pool:
Q. As	a matter	of	fact	you	never	had
occasion as chief commissioner to confer with the advisory committee at all?
That is the advisory committee to the board which the act provided for, and which was done away with when Mr. Murray accepted the position.
It was not obligatory.

The question was:
Q. As	a matter	of	fact	you	never	had
occasion as chief commissioner to confer with the advisory committee at all?
A. No.

Q. Was that your recommendation, or was that, again, a matter of governmental policy?
A. I stated that I would not accept the position of chief commissioner with any advisory board.
Q. So that your appointment was really contingent on the determination of this committee's life?
A. As far as I was concerned.
Q. And consequently you were appointed chief commissioner and the advisory committee as provided in the act ceased to exist?
A. Yes. The government had the choice, of course.
Q. Oh yes, I am not questioning that. That was during pleasure.
A. No, but I mean they had the choice of getting some one else for chief commissioner and keeping the advisory committee.
Then comes this last question:
Q. Yes. They had the choice of either taking you without the committee or getting somebody else with the committee?
A. Yes.
Q. I am submitting this, that you as a matter of principle refused to act as chief commissioner of the wheat board with the advisory committee as provided for in the act?
A. Yes.
I make this comment, Mr. Chairman, that had the advisory committee been there, Mr. Murray never would have sold the 22,000,000 bushels on the morning of the thirteenth when the market price of Argentine wheat had also gone up that same morning. That is proof that Mr. Murray dictated terms, and I believe that all the time he was operating he proved himself to be a dictator.
I could quote further from his evidence, if I desire to take the time, to show that he was also very inconsistent. I should not like to refer to him in the terms in which he referred to some hon. members of this house, but I could cite evidence to prove that he was in a similar position himself. In fact he stated on page 162 of the 1936 evidence, on April 28, "that the agreement that was made with the exchange was purely a verbal one." I myself had asked him whether there was any written statement or agreement, and he said no, it was purely a verbal one.
At page 259 of that evidence, on May 1, the leader of the opposition read into the evidence the agreement that had been made with the members of the exchange. In answer to the leader of the opposition Mr. Murray admitted that the agreement was made on the twelfth, and he stated that the suggestion came from the members of the Winnipeg grain committee. The concluding part of the paragraph reads:
The board agrees with the suggestion made by the exchange.
On page 196 of this report, in answer to questions put to him by Mr. Ralston, Mr. Murray admitted that he himself had made

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
the approach and been the first to suggest that there should be a meeting with the members of the exchange, and further that he was the only member of the board who was present at that meeting when the agreement was made. Reference is made on page 196 to the meeting with the exchange and that Mr. Murray was the only member of the board to meet with the members of the grain exchange.
At page 198 of the report Mr. Murray refers to the fact that the board knew what was likely to take place in connection with the Argentine government. They had known, for several days before, of the action of the Argentine government, and they knew also on the morning of the thirteenth what action the Argentine government had taken, and they expected the increase-there is no question about that.
I should like to remind the committee at this point that what are known as the Big Three, that is Dreyfus and Company, Bunge and Company and the Continental were operating very extensively in the Argentine. Bunge and Dreyfus controlled practically all the wheat at that time before it was taken over at the price fixed by the Argentine government. Is it not fair to assume, then, that they would know what was likely to take place when the government of the Argentine was taking over the wheat and setting the price? It is only reasonable to suppose that they would know. They had acquainted their branch office in Winnipeg with the fact that word had come from the New York office, and no doubt their representatives in Winnipeg knew of it. I myself have seen a letter-I do not propose to give the name right now-written by the manager of a large United States firm, complaining that they were not being tipped off like some of the other large firms, and stating that they knew certain gentlemen had been dispatched from New York to Winnipeg to negotiate with their firm there and to acquaint many of the Winnipeg firms with what was likely to take place. All sorts of evidence could have been produced to show that they knew.
On page 197 of this report Mr. Murray was giving evidence and he admitted to Mr. Ralston that the agreement made with the exchange was new and quite unprecedented; that there was no precedent for it at all. Here is the evidence:
Q. Was an arrangement of this kind new as far as you know in the history of the grain trade?
A. Yes, it -was new as far as the government was concerned.
Then he goes on to say:
In so far as it was an arrangement entered into with all people who were interested in the grain business.
There was no precedent for such an arrangement. In my opinion, if they had called certain witnesses, they could have proved that there was knowledge of what was going on. When the question was before the committee Mr. Murray was the only witness heard, and we asked for proof of sale so far as the grain firms were concerned, but no evidence was produced before the committee.
I believe the minister will recall that he himself asked me whether all the evidence I had asked for as to proof of sale had been produced, and I said no. I said that the offers and acceptances, which were the main proof of sale, had not been presented to the committee. He must remember that.
Then we had the auditors' report-I have it here-which definitely states that in their search of the records they were unable to find proof of sale of 703,000 bushels. With respect to several hundred thousand bushels there was never any proof of sale, and it was delivered by the board to the grain people. The auditors' report is conclusive proof also that wheat was delivered without real proof of sale. What I am about to say is, I think, important. It is this. When Mr. Murray was being examined with regard to this transaction, as will be seen in the evidence, they only asked him two or three questions. First, they asked him whether he knew that there was a short interest in the market, and his reply was that he was not concerned whether there was or not. They asked him whether he knew, when he made the sales, that he was protecting the short interest, and his reply to Mr. Ralston, on page 190 and page 200 of the report, was that he did not know. Those were practically all the questions asked him-that is, pertinent questions.
Then Mr. Mclvor was called. He was an accomplice in the crime, so to speak, and he was asked similar questions. He was asked, "Did you know there was a shortage?" And his answer was, "No." Then they asked him, "Did you know they were protecting the shorts?" And his answer was, "No." The other witness was Dean Shaw, that innocent chap from Saskatchewan. He was called in and asked the same questions. These three witnesses were all asked the same questions, and their answers were, "No." I contend that, though they did not have any more witnesses than the wheat committee had, we got just as far. We had Mr. Murray and we asked him these questions, and we had more proof of the fact that he knew that there was a short interest than Mr. Ralston apparently was able to bring out. I would remind the



Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
committee of the attitude of Hon. J. L. Ralston when he was accusing Mr. McFarland. When he was in opposition he tried to hang Mr. McFarland, so to speak. He tried to pin certain charges upon him. Here we have him, this hangman, in a different role. He has three prisoners before him and you can almost see the hangman's rope under his gown and the noose sticking out. But on this occasion, speaking to the prisoner, he says: "Did you think when you were clubbing this fellow that you were murdering him?" What would you expect the prisoner to say in reply? He asked Mr. Murray, charged with protecting shorts, "Did you think that you were protecting shorts when you sold the wheat?" What would anyone expect Mr. Murray to say? It was the biggest farce ever perpetrated on the people of Canada, and the people are asked to pay for it.

That is strong
language.

Yes, but it is a fact. They should have called the members of the large grain companies whom we had asked to have before the committee, and there should have been a proper accounting of the books to trace the sales. If they had done that they would have got somewhere. But simply to call these three men and ask them the questions I have indicated was certainly a farce.
There were other questions that were referred to the commission but I do not think it is necessary to take up much time discussing them. There was the Saskatchewan oat deal. The problem was definite: who was responsible for the loss? This report sets aside for all time any difficulty in that connection inasmuch as it places responsibility for the loss of $163,000 upon the government of Saskatchewan during the time that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was premier. The evidence shows that they were speculating. They bought eight millions of options, two millions more than it was estimated that they would require, and they knew it; and they paid Gordon Brown $4,500 to manage this operation in which they took a loss of the sum I have stated, $163,000.
The question of a barley comer was referred to the commission, but I will not discuss that. The statement in the report is not correct that barley advanced only 10 cents in the month of December, because it advanced 29 cents. As regards the Saskatchewan oat deal, it might have been interesting to call the Minister of Agriculture, because he knew more about it than any other man, and his evidence might have thrown some light on the subject. 
There is a certain recommendation with regard to the continuance of the -board, and the recommendation is also made that small pools be set up. Well, we know what happened to the small pools, and we know what happened to the main pool. When there is competition with the strong interests, the recommendation of small pools is ridiculous because they could not operate at all.
I suggest that the inquiry should have been more thorough than it was. When the committee was set up we asked that a thorough investigation be made, and on March 30, 1937, dealing with the matter in the house, I myself asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he would see to it that the inquiry made should be full and complete. The right hon. leader of the opposition also made certain statements along that line, and we had a reply from the minister that he would endeavour to put the ease before the commission and let us know what happened. I have certain correspondence here, too long to read in its entirety, but it is so important that I feel justified in reading some of it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was good enough to say to me on March 30 last year that he would endeavour to see that the inquiry was as thorough as possible and that the case was placed before the commissioner, which was done. I asked for this correspondence at the opening of this session, and it was tabled, so it is all on the record.
The first letter is from the deputy minister to Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, Royal Grain Inquiry Commission, and dated April 5, 1937, as follows:
Dear Judge Turgeon:
Mr. Euler has asked me to forward to you the enclosed copy of Hansard for Tuesday, March 30, commencing on page 254 of which you will find the discussion that took place in the house with reference to an item "Expenses of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission" in our supplementary estimates for 1936-37.
You will observe the remarks by Mr. Perley (Qu'Appelle) and by the Rt. Hon. Mr. Bennett in regard to the oats deal by the Saskatchewan government in 1935, a reference to the corner on barley and a direct inquiry by the Rt. Hon. Mr. Bennett as to whether the commission would investigate the grain and elevator companies that acquired stocks of grain at the lake ports and their profits. Mr. Euler stated that he would bring these comments to your attention.
Will you kindly let me know, for the information of the minister, whether or not these matters have been or are likely to be dealt with by the commission and if not, your views in that connection?
There is a lengthy reply addressed to the deputy minister, dated April 16. There are some important paragraphs. It acknowledges

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
receipt of the letter of April 5 and enclosed copy of Hansard, and states that the delay in reply was due to the fact that the letter was sent to Vancouver and had to be returned to Edmonton. It states that the commission is authorized to inquire into and report on-
All transactions since the year 1930 pertaining to the handling of grain for relief and seeding purposes in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta under the dominion government guarantee, or otherwise.
And continues:
It is anticipated that evidence will be taken on this phase of the inquiry when the commission sits in Regina, probably early in May.
Secondly, there has been some reference in the evidence already taken to what Mr. Perley mentioned as a "corner on barley."
They say they are going to take evidence with respect to that when they get to Winnipeg. The reply continues:
Thirdly, I am not quite clear regarding the nature and scope of the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett's proposal that we should investigate the "grain and elevator companies that acquired stocks of grain at the lake ports and their profits as was done in the case of the textile companies and ascertain what happened in connection with the rest of the crop that was sold in connection with which there was a loss of $15,000,000, though there appears now to have been a profit of $8,000,000."
Then he says Mr. Bennett expressed the view that the commission should-
"investigate the various grain companies that acquired from the grain board, presided over by Mr. Murray, the wheat that was at the lake ports and should ascertain who owned that wheat, the visible supply 'in Canada at the present time."
And following Hon. Mr. Euler's question: "Any particular time?" Rt. Hon. Mr. Bennett replied:
"At this time, before the opening of navigation. The commission should ascertain who owns the wheat and should investigate the accounts, showing the profits with respect to these transactions."
Then a further paragraph:
The proposal quoted appears to involve following through the grain and futures disposed of by the board and ascertaining what amount of such grain now constitutes part of the present visible supply in Canada and by whom it is owned, and the financial result of the transactions so far as the purchasers from the board are concerned. It is not considered that such an inquiry is contemplated by P.C. 1577.
But quite apart from the order in council it would appear that such an inquiry would he altogether impracticable as it would involve an attempt to trace through and segregate the ultimate results of individual transactions respecting parcels of wheat or futures which, up to July 31,	1936, aggregated upwards of
100,000,000 bushels and covered, even up to that date, a period of about 200 trading days.

In addition to segregating the transactions in these parcels from purchases by the individuals concerned from other sources, there is the factor that in following through to ascertain the financial result to the purchaser the wheat covered by the $15,000,000 and $8,000,000 referred to would have to be distinguished in the purchaser's accounts from 1935-36 crop wheat purchased from the board, and it seems apparent that this could not be done. An attempt to follow through specific transactions in futures would seem to be even more futile.
Then it winds up:
For the reasons given above such an inquiry is not contemplated, any more than it is contemplated that the financial results to purchasers from the pools or the central selling agency would be gone into. Without, of course, prejudicing the matter, it would rather seem as if the transactions might be more logically appraised by conditions existing and reasonably to be forecast at the time of the transactions than by post hoc developments.
Now there is a statement by Judge Tur-geon himself that he did not propose to make a thorough investigation.
I have numerous other letters here. That letter was acknowledged; the minister suggested to Judge Turgeon that he would like to refer the letters to Mr. Bennett and myself, and he got consent to do so. The letter directed to myself, dated April 22, 1937 reads as follows:
I am directed by the minister to forward you herewith for your information copies of correspondence between Mr. Justice Turgeon and myself, relating to questions asked in the House of Commons on March 30 last by the right hon. Mr. Bennett and yourself with respect to certain phases of the inquiry.
Attached is a copy of my letter of April 5 to Judge Turgeon, and copy of his reply, which is dated April 16. The right hon. Mr. Bennett has also been provided with copies of this correspondence.
That is from the deputy minister. I have the answer that the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett made to a similar letter addressed to himself dated April 26, in which he said:
I am wholly dissatisfied with the answer made by Judge Turgeon and you may so inform him. If he could deal with the balance sheets of the textile companies as he has he certainly could deal with the balance sheets of the elevator and other grain companies so as to show what, if any, profit -was made by them through the acquisition of grain from the wheat board, assuming that the grain so

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
acquired has since been disposed of. No one was suggesting that he should investigate the handling of 'the 100,000,000 bushels of grain, and I doubt if anyone knows that more clearly than he does himself. I merely suggested that he apply the same principles in dealing with the grain companies as he did in dealing with the textile companies. There was a large quantity of grain owned by grain companies east of Fort William over the winter season of 1937. When was it bought, from whom, and what profit was made on it? Those questions really cover what I had in mind when I was speaking in the house.
I have the correspondence that took place between Colonel Ralston and myself. I replied to that letter setting out what I intended when I asked that the inquiry be thorough. My letter was also referred to Colonel Ralston, and I have here a two-hundred word lettergram from Colonel Ralston. The final words are:
If there are further matters which you think are within scope of commission and are not already being covered, would you kindly write giving definite particulars of what you have in mind.
In reply I sent a five page letter, which I am not going to take time to read, but which I can summarize in this way: I said I thought the inquiry should be thorough; that they should proceed along the lines that had been followed in connection with the textile commission, where Judge Turgeon was also commissioner. I cited what the implement committee had done in connection with sending auditors to the head offices of the implement companies in order to audit their books and bring the statements back to the committee. I also told Mr. Ralston that from my experience with him on two important committees of this house he was beginning to know the grain business pretty well; that he had the ability and that, if he so desired, he could assist the judge in making this a thorough inquiry. In reply I received a statement from the auditors. Colonel Ralston stated that Price Waterhouse and Company had audited certain books of the exchange. They made reference to certain paragraphs in letters from myself and the leader of the opposition, as well as the books of certain firms. Rut really there were no official audits made. They went and asked these companies to show them their books and accounts, and finally stated to the committee that they did not think a further audit was necessary, that it would require quite a period of time and that it would involve following through the different accounts. Then they made the statement, in regard to the sixty-two million bushel transaction that I have cited in July, in order to show how difficult it would be

to trace those sales, that during the month of July there had been 640,000,000 bushels traded in. In other words, the whole crop had been bought and sold three times during that month.
So, Mr. Chairman, I think there is proof conclusive that they never intended to make this a thorough inquiry. Certainly they did not examine the members of the exchange as we desired. In one of my letters I suggested that they might examine the books of the "big three," to see what influence they had on the market, and also that their transactions might be traced.
Now I desire to take just a little time to deal with the recommendations and suggestions that have been made. As I stated a moment ago the commission recommended that small pools be set up to carry on and that the wheat board stand by. When they made the recommendation concerning the wheat board I say that' was an admission of failure, as far as the Winnipeg Grain Exchange was concerned. Let me say here that Mr. Richardson, Mr. Sydney Smith, Mr. Milner, and others who gave evidence before the committee in 1935, suggested that somebody should stand by with a basket to take up the slack in case of an emergency, as Mr. McFarland had done. Now the commission recommends that the board stand by, for this season at least, in case of an emergency. Then the recommendation is made that there be some supervision of the grain exchange. Practically all the witnesses agreed on that. At page 9242 of the evidence Mr. Murray said there should foe some machinery for supervision, similar to that recommended by the Stamp commission. Mr. Paul Mehl, senior agricultural economist, at page 11211 of the evidence, said at Chicago that exchange selfgovernment did not meet the situation in the United States, and that there should be some control. Mr. Darby, secretary of the grain exchange, speaking for the exchange, said that supervision such as the Stamp commission recommended would be good. Mr. Taggart, a farmer from Gull Lake, Saskatchewan, said there should be some supervision of the exchange to prevent raids on the futures market. Mr. Mathieson, speaking of Chicago, said Chicago was no more difficult to trade in than Winnipeg, yet Chicago had supervision. Mr. McFarland, dealing with the type of supervision suggested by the previous witnesses, at page 7626 stated that he did not think it would be of any use whatever, that a supervisor of that kind would be like a guest in the clearing house.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
With regard to the need for supervision, evidence was given of raids, by the "big three" in particular, on the Winnipeg exchange. The Stamp commission took evidence with respect to the amount of trading carried on during a given period, and also with respect to raids made from time to time on the market. In that evidence an interesting fact was brought out. They took the year 1929, which was considered an average crop year, when we had
304.000.	000 bushels of wheat in western Canada. They found that during that year there had been 7,200,000,000 bushels of wheat traded in. The period taken was from May 1, 1929, to March 31, 1930. Taking that as including some three hundred trading days, there was an average of about 24,000,000 bushels traded in each day. The crop, as I have said, totalled
304.000.	000 bushels. That year the pools handled 121,000,000 bushels which did not need to be hedged and did not go through the market. There were 50,000,000 bushels retained for seed, so the hedgeable grain from that crop amounted to only 133,000,000 bushels. The carry-over from the previous year was
91.000.	000 bushels, of which a certain amount was controlled by the pools, leaving only 43,000,000 bushels available for hedging purposes. This gave a total of 176,000,000 bushels of wheat available for hedging during that period in 1929, but the grain exchange traded in 7,-
200,000,000 bushels. In other words they bought and sold the crop forty-one times.
I just want to ask any hon. member of this house in his right senses, particularly any farmer member, if he thinks it is necessary to have an organization that will buy and sell a crop forty-one times in order to market
176.000.	000 bushels of cash grain. I do not think it is necessary, and I think they were wise when they suggested some supervision and control.
Now I want to refer to the question of speculation and the cost of hedging, in connection with which a number of witnesses were examined. Sir Robert Robson appeared before the Stamp commission and said that as a result of speculators losing money gambling in wheat in Chicago, he thought the people in England got their grain much cheaper. Mr. Sydney Smith referred to speculating on the Winnipeg market. He said, "I think the great majority was held by farmers. Farmers are speculators, merchants are speculators;" everybody was speculating. I do not think that should be permitted.
Then there were numerous other witnesses who gave evidence as to what speculation costs Canada. Mr. Poloway, of the Dauphin district made a statement to the effect that the farmers of his district in the year 1929-30
had lost $970,000. We have the informed and the uninformed public among the witnesses who were examined. Mr. Murray himself said that Canada was only looking in its own backyard. Mr. Darby answered the question as to who would be competent speculators. He stated they would be the members of the Winnipeg exchange, and stated that the uninformed public were the farmers, stenographers and clerks.
Mr. Dowler gave evidence that they had to have these speculators in the market in order to set an average or proper price representing the value of wheat. I say you cannot have a fair market or a fair price when you have a market of speculators who, as has been shown by the evidence-and I should like to quote it further-are not competent judges. How is it possible that a price registration which depends upon an unknown volume of unintelligent speculators can be said to record as accurate an estimate of present values as can be achieved, as was suggested by Mr. Dowler of the exchange?
I have much evidence before me as to what would happen if the Winnipeg market closed. Mr. David Muir of Glasgow stated that he would see no difficulty if the futures market closed. Mr. Stoik of Antwerp, a broker, when asked what difference it would make to his purchases of Canadian wheat, could not see that it would .make any difference; that it would be just one less to deal with. Snodgrass of Glasgow said that if the Winnipeg market disappeared and the futures market were to close, he could, get along quite well without it. Mr. Bracey, an English buyer for the Scottish Wholesale Cooperative at Liverpool, said this would be a good procedure, and that the advantage would be to the producer.
There were many others whose statements I could give if I had the time. I submit the price of our wheat on the Liverpool market must ultimately prove to be a better basic bargaining start than the futures market. I should have liked to have time to deal with some other aspects of the matter. I should like to tell what the farmers who came before the commission said, when they stated their case. However, I do not wish to take too much time along that line.
I have some evidence before me in the report with respect to the operations of the "big three." I have evidence from a British witness who said that the "big three" had driven the small man out of the Liverpool market. I submit therefore that a business which is so important to the national life of Canada as is the marketing of wheat; which has been the subject of seventeen royal grain

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
inquiries in thirty-seven years; which is carried on under rules and regulations of an exchange subject to the control of nobody outside; which does not know the volume of hedging transactions as distinct from speculation carried on in its trading room; which does not know who operates on its market, or if there are any large manipulative traders; which refuses to divulge the volume of business conducted on its premises, and which is subject to outside investigation only by royal commission with respect to the conduct of its affairs-any such business must be a proper subject for strict and full governmental supervision.
I say the supervision recommended in the commission report does not go far enough. I regret at this session the minister is not even going to move concurrence in the report, or take action with respect to it to implement some of the suggestions made therein. I therefore make the following recommendations:
1.	That a national grain board be put into force to operate under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and that all coarse grains be brought under the operation of the act. I would even go so far as to suggest that the act be enlarged to take in all grain products.
2.	That grain merchants and elevator companies operate as at present, doing a general grain business on the open market.
3.	That there be supervision by a board of the operations of the exchange and the Winnipeg Grain Clearing house, in the following manner:
Said board to be a branch of the board of grain commissioners, and to be composed of three members-the chairman of the board of grain commissioners to be the chairman- and two other members, one of whom would be appointed by the producers and one by the grain dealers. This branch of the grain commissioners would have full control and operate the clearing house. They would license all members, grant a line of credit for trading purposes, set rates of commissions and clearing charges, and have control of the amount of future trades that could be cleared in proportion to the amount of actual cash grain handled by each individual trader.
In conclusion I submit that the grain act should be amended, and that the wheat board act should be put into full force and carried out at once. I protest against the failure of the Turgeon commission to bring out the facts with respect to trading through the Winnipeg clearing association, although we had asked that that be done.

We are now being asked to vote a sum to meet the further costs of the commission which was set up more than two years ago and headed by Judge Turgeon, who receives a judge's allowance of $9,000 a year and $35 per day for living and travelling expenses. The commission retained Mr. Ralston at $200 a day and expenses, and paid an assistant $50 per day, and $10 per day for expenses. They had a very expensive staff. May I point out further that that is not the whole cost of the commission so far as the people of Canada are concerned. We know that the commission was followed by nineteen other counsel, four or five of whom were leading men such as Mr. Brockington, Mr. Pitblado and Mr. MacPherson. Certainly someone has to pay for that, and the payment will fall on the people of Canada.
After taking evidence in 1937 the commission filed a report on May 9 of this year. I say we should have had the report before us in time to deal with it properly at this session. The commission began their sittings in Ottawa, and then moved to Fort Wiliam, Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver, then returning to the Atlantic seaboard. They went overseas and sat in London, Liverpool, Antwerp and other places. They sat and sat and sat and sat for almost two years. Who would not sit and and sit if he were getting $200 a day and expenses to tour Great Britain, the continent and all of Canada?
All this was at great expense to the pools. The pools had to send their representatives. What is the value of the report? What value can there be attached to a report on which no action is taken-a report I am inclined to believe that the wheat committee of this government reviewed and sent back a time or two.
What is that?
I believe the wheat committee reviewed the report before it was printed and before it was tabled, and reported it back to be revised.
Absolutely untrue.

I have anticipated the minister's statement. But reports we have received would lead us to believe that. I am led to believe that from the comments by members of the Winnipeg grain exchange the morning the report was tabled in the house, comments which lead us to believe that someone there knew something about it. However, that is something that possibly cannot be proved.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
There are other things that cannot be proved also.

We are facing an emergency and we should have a statement from the minister before this vote passes as to what he proposes to do this fall. The pool representatives have been down here negotiating with the government. We have a crop in prospect but we are facing an emergency. We want the wheat board. We want a fixed minimum price of from 87 to 90 cents. We want participation certificates, and we want the personnel of the board changed so that it will have the confidence of the producers. We want an advisory committee set up. That was the one protection the farmer had, when he had four representatives on the committee. Why should fourteen or fifteen Liberal members of this house be going back to Saskatchewan with a promise in their vest pockets of a wheat board? Reports have been going around that these fourteen or fifteen members swallowed this promise and agreed to vote for the budget. They were given the promise that they were going to have a wheat board, and they are taking back that promise. We should have a statement made right here so that we will know what is to happen. The farmers have a right to know.

speechtext: I think I should take exception at once to what the hon. member has said about any promise having been made to western members with respect to a wheat board. Nothing of the kind was ever suggested.
The western members made the promise.

I was led to believe that there was quite an interesting caucus held. If the reports I received were right-they may not be-but the western members understood that they were going to have a wheat board and they promised that they would come into this house and vote for the budget if they got a wheat board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Apart from the impropriety of referring to what takes place in a party caucus, may I say to my hon. friend-

Personal and private
letters are no longer private.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The subject was never discussed in a Liberal caucus. That is the answer to what my hon. friend has said.
Some of the Liberal members may have gained the wrong impression, because they have said they are going to have a wheat board.
The announcement was made by myself that there would be a wheat board, and it was said that the price would be fixed later on. That statement was made weeks ago.

I should like the minister to substantiate that by stating that we are going to have a real board functioning under the act. I want him to tell us that we are to have a minimum price, that we are to have participation certificates. If we are not going to have a wheat board, I think the pools should know so that they will have an opportunity of organizing.
The pools will not operate if there is a wheat board. There is going to be a wheat board. They knew that, and my hon. friend knew that.
I regret very much that we have not had an opportunity to discuss the 1936-37 report of the wheat board, signed on January 6, 1938. The time has been much too short.

You will have another
opportunity if you want it.
In conclusion let me say again that the money spent on this report is absolutely wasted. We knew most of what is contained in the report long before they ever began to take evidence.

I do not know
whether I agree with what has been said by the hon. member who just sat down (Mr. Perley) as I did not hear much of it. I heard a few words like "McFarland," "carryover," "shorts and longs" and "overages," but I did not hear anything about "fire sale."
The evidence of that is here also.

We must use every shining hour, yea minute if we are to get out of here this afternoon. I am going to talk until one o'clock as a sort of cocktail before lunch. I do not take them myself, but I know some other hon. members appreciate them. As I understand it, there are two items before the committee, Nos. 372 and 373. I want to say a word or two on item No. 375. There are four items here that are identical and intertwined, one with the other, and I think they should be considered as one. I have my dope arranged in that way and I do not want to disarrange it. The chairman has assured me that I can make any reference to grain I desire under vote 372.
Transport Commission

The first item refers particularly to the' royal grain commission, and I think I can say what I think of that commission in two words, yes two letters, I think it is "N.G," but must as I go along give my reasons for so thinking. We all remember the remarkable unanimity there was in committee of the whole when the Wheat Board Act of 1935 was under discussion, and when it received its third reading. I think it would have been a good thing if that unanimity had continued. This matter has been ushered into the realm of politics by the order in council objected to. Why is so much being said about this problem now? It is due to the fact that while the present government was joint father of the wheat board act, it has committed infanticide or at least has mutilated the foster child to such a degree that it might as well be dead. This act is simply an ornament on our statute books.

It is an ornamental
statute.

I know some hon. members want a fairly good cocktail. This act received unanimous support at that time and I think every effort should be made to continue that feeling of unanimity. Certainly things should not have been changed to such an extent without the consent of this parliament. I should like to quote from a speech made by my right hon. leader at Calgary on September 30, 1935.
