subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT -CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 31, to establish a board of transport commissioners for Canada, with authority in respect of transport by railways, ships and aircraft.
He said: This bill has been returned with its tail-feathers rather clipped. It is not the bill which this chamber adopted; still, there is something left.

In the interpretation clause several changes have been made. Two further definitions have been added. Waste paper loaded as full ship's cargo has been put in the list for exemption from regulation. To that there is no particular objection.
The changes are principally in part I, in relation to transport by water.
As a subsection of section 3 the following has been included:
(2) It shall be the duty of the board to perform the functions vested in the board by this act and by the Railway Act with the object of coordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, ships and aircraft, and the board shall give to this act and to the Railway Act such fair interpretation as will best attain the object aforesaid.
That is not material. However, section 5 has been changed by practically eliminating the convenience and necessity provision. It is provided that any boat that can indicate that at any time within the last ten years it has been engaged in carrying any item of package freight will be entitled to a certificate of convenience and necessity under the grandfather clause. Some forty boats are actually and exclusively engaged in package freight, and some 150 other boats are now eligible to engage in it, so that the certificate of convenience and necessity will not have any particular meaning with these amendments added.
Then an amendment has been added which exempts from the operation of the act shipping between the Pacific coast and the Atlantic coast. I think that that is unfortunate, because by putting this traffic outside the scope of the act, it does not enable those engaged in it to protest agreed charges which may affect the traffic of the ships in that service.
However, the bill has been reported with those changes. Aside from those I have mentioned there are, I believe, no material changes. As I have said, in my opinion it is not as good a bill as went to the senate, but after a good deal of consideration I have decided to ask the concurrence of the house in the senate amendments.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

To provide for expenses of the royal grain inquiry commission, including authority for payment of honorarium to Dr. T. W. Grindley, secretary, $15,000.

Supply-Trade-Gram Commission

When the committee rose for lunch I was about to read the report of a speech made at Swift Current by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). But I think I will defer that for a moment, and deal with what, I believe, should come before that, namely, the ill-fated order in council with the worse than ill-fated rider thereon-*

Hear, hear. Without
authority of law.

-which not only
sterilizes the bill but caponizes it also. I pronounced "caponizing" with a long "a"; but no matter whether you use the long "a" or the short "a", it and "sterilizing" mean the same thing to the bill, because they render it innocuous.
It has been the most distressing experience of my whole life that a Liberal government should do this. Would to the Most High that it had been the Tories who had been responsible for it, or yon strange people in the corner. I could have put up with it, not easily, but at least without agony. What has come over the government? Wait till I read this fatal abuse of executive power. Well, it is too long to read it all.
Remember first that when this order in council was launched across the prairie it created such consternation and resentment that I have never seen the like of it. What was that about? Because an order in council had been passed which thwarted the will of this parliament-
Hear, hear.
-and nullified it, -passed by a Liberal government, no less.
No more!

I have not the
patience to read the blamed thing. We have on our files 174 bills passed this year, or which will soon have been passed, by this house. If the executive can pass this kind of order in council and get away with it, not one of the bills which passed this year is safe from the dexterity of similar orders in council passed here by an expert hand. Why have these 174 bills been passed? What do we gather here for? Might we not just as well have a Mussolini and be through with it? Why this assembly at all? I have been down in the West Indies for a time recovering from one of this kind of fights. Down there the governor, of course, is boss. But surely in Canada the days of governor bosses have gone and we have something like democracy.
I do not know where to start, reading for most convenience, but I will quote the following :
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated August 27, 1936, from the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, stating that under clause A of section 8 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, provision is made that it shall be the duty of the Canadian wheat board, established under the said act, to fix the price to be paid to the producers of wheat delivered to the board as by the said act provided, subject to the approval of the governor general in council:
That the Canadian wheat board, established under the said act, has fixed a price of eighty-seven and one-half cents (87i cents) per bushel for wheat graded as No. 1 Northern at Fort William, as a basis price for wheat for the 1936-37 crop year, effective from August 1, 1936, delivered to the board as provided by the said act, the price of other grades of wheat to be fixed by the board on the basis of the price for No. 1 Northern wheat delivered at Fort William as aforesaid;
Then for some strange reason it makes reference to the appointment of the royal grain commission. I do not think that it is necessary to read that; the committee will take it for granted. The appointment of a commission! The very thing that should have warned the government against meddling in this matter. And then the government take this important part-grain marketing- away from the commission and decide it themselves, when the problem is sub judice. I think, after all, I had better read it:
That the Honourable William Ferdinand Alphonse Turgeon of Regina, Sask., a judge of the court of appeal of Saskatchewan, was appointed a commissioner under part I of the Inquiries Act, being chapter 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, to inquire into and to report upon the subject of the production, buying, selling, holding, storing, transporting and exporting of Canadian grains and grain products, and other questions incident to such matters, and in particular, but without restricting the generality of the foregoing terms, to inquire into and to report upon:
The methods now or heretofore employed in marketing Canadian grains abroad, including government grain boards, cooperative or pool marketing, price stabilization measures and the open market or competitive method; and the effect of these various methods upon markets;
The measures which should be taken to retain and to extend the marketing throughout the world of Canadian wheat and other grains and their products.
The minister, therefore, recommends that the recommendations of the Canadian wheat board be not approved unconditionally but that approval be given only in the event of the closing market price for wheat dropping below ninety cents per bushel for wheat graded as No. 1 Northern at Fort William, in which event a price of 87i cents per bushel as recommended by the board shall be approved, and this order in council be regarded as approving the same.
444S

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
That is the rider that did the trick; that is the rider that defies parliament; and in my estimation it will be very bad for the authors thereof. The order in council last year was different; it left out the reference to the royal commission. Let me tell you the consternation with which this action was received throughout the prairies. I first heard about it on a Saturday night and I refused to believe it. I thought it was some fool report across the wires such as we sometimes get, some mistake; and it was not until Monday morning that I discovered when I went to deliver my wheat to the pool elevator for the board that I could not do it, after working hard with others to get this method of marketing satisfactorily established. I was not on the special committee, but outside I was helping to get the bill through in order that we might have a piece of legislation about which there would be no controversy. I am familiar enough with law to know that if you get all parties behind an act you are well away with the administration of it; but if the people are split in two, one-half bucking the other, then you will have difficulty in administering your law. The matter should have been left as it was until this parliament could make any change deemed necessary. It should not have been done by order in council or any such reprehensible method. It should, I repeat, have been done by this parliament and not otherwise. I have no language to describe the horror of the people, especially the Liberals. We were used to hearing these things about the Tories governing by order in council, and whatever the Tories do is always wrong anyhow-we are always safe, so it is averred, in that assumption. But regardless of politics, right across those stricken prairies, like a bolt from the blue went roars of indignation that can almost be heard to-day. I am trying to reverberate them a little. You do not need to be told about the popular indignation in the prairies, and I cannot adequately describe it.
Dozens and possibly hundreds of telegrams and letters were sent to the ministry. I myself sent three of them, and in those telegrams I left nothing unsaid. It would have cost the same to send a wishy-washy telegram or letter as to send a good one and the good one went. In addition to these messages all the municipal organizations, all the agricultural societies, within and throughout the prairies, the provincial government of Saskatchewan in session assembled, and the province of Manitoba -all these various bodies made representations against the emasculated wheat board. The province of Saskatchewan two years in succes-

sion passed resolutions on the question asking for a wheat board, and I believe that they had in mind not a sterilized but a real one. They did not designate. The province of Manitoba said that they wanted a real, live wheat board, one that would not hibernate twelve months in the year. Notwithstanding all this, in this democratic country, the government stood obdurate. We all like the idea that once a man has put his hand to the plough he should not turn back; but when you have put your hand to a plough with crooked handles the quicker one turns back the better and easier is the turning.
With such an order in council as that, look at the danger and likelihood there was in appointing a royal commission which would in all probability take its cue from that order. And that is what they did, and that is the kind of report we got. It was the will of the government expressed there in that order in council. Let me say a word about the appointment of the commissioner. A good many foolish people talk about the vast amount of money spent for the commissioner and his counsel, but if we had got value the price was not too high; if, on the other hand, we have not got value, then the money was wasted. I do not think it was fair to commissioner Turgeon to appoint him as sole commissioner. Ever since the first chairman of a royal grain commission was appointed, Judge Sinclair of Perth in the county of Lanark- my birthplace, by the way-ever since he was appointed to the first grain commission in 1898 or 1899, I forget which, there have never been fewer than three commissioners investigating these many sided grain problems until the last one of 1936. And even with the united efforts of all these we have never yet had a grain act that the grain mixers at the head of the lakes and elsewhere could not drive a coach and four through if they were any kind of teamsters at all. I do not think any living man alone can do justice to an inquiry of this nature with such extensive ramifications. I repeat. I do not think it was fair to Mr. Justice Turgeon. There was much to be inquired into about the technique of terminal elevators. I wonder if Justice Turgeon or any of his counsel were ever in a terminal elevator. They certainly got as far away as they could from the depredations that I am going to speak about presently; trying to investigate an elevator at the head of the lakes from Vancouver is a new stunt to me. That is all I will say about the commissioner, except to repeat that no man living can properly investigate a great

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
question like the grain trade with the doors of inquiry wide open, as expressed in the order in council.
And what about the counsel? Who says aught against the ability of Colonel Ralston? Not I. But I have a little to say about the propriety of both the giving of it and of his taking it. It is not considered good form- I may be getting on legal ground with which I am not too familiar-but the very last act of Colonel Ralston as reported in the proceedings of the special committee of 1935 on the Canada Grain Board Act was to move an amendment to the bill as section 10, namely:
The operations of the board shall not extend beyond the 15th day of August 1936 except for the purpose of sale and realization of assets, collections, payments, and generally for the winding up of the affairs and business of the board, unless on or before the first day of July 1936 the operation of this act be extended by order of the governor in council for one year from the date first mentioned in this section, in which event such operations with the exception above mentioned shall terminate on August 15, 1937, unless further extended by parliament.
That was Colonel Ralston's view. Anyone who has expressed himself so freely and publicly surely should not have -been appointed counsel on the commission. If Colonel Ralston or any hon. member here present had been summoned to act on a jury, and had said as much about the subject before the jury as Colonel Ralston did about this, the other side would have challenged his right to sit on the jury. There is not a lawyer in this chamber who does not know that. Of course the claim may be made that this royal commission is not the same as a court. But it had all the frills and all the authority of a court. This order in council was passed when the question was sub judice before that court, and the government grabbed off a maximum chunk of it and decided it themselves pending the report of the commission. We have never heard the like in the history of Canada. If I am to hear and see much more like that I am not caring when I pass out. The disgrace to our country! Colonel Ralston is one of the finest men that you can meet in a day's journey, but this is not the place for him. His price is not of so much concern, the $200 a day, but it is the getting the whole thing in the hands of the government: one commissioner, one master counsel, and presto! you can get any kind of report you like. That is what happened anyhow.
Now that is something like the kind of indignation that was aroused when this whole distressing incident was first noised abroad. The Prime Minister is, I feel sure, averse to all this-and I want to say incidentally that I
do not lay one iota of this at the door of the Prime Minister. But he cannot avoid his responsibility. He has some mighty bad advisers or rather a bad adviser around him in regard to the grain business. This is generally known to be true, but opinions may differ as to who constitutes a good adviser. This is from a press despatch report of a speech delivered by the Prime Minister at Calgary on September 30, 1935:
Farmers were just as much entitled to fixed prices for their products as labour was to fixed minimum wages. Mr. King said he believed in fixing these levels for the purpose of maintaining standards of living. But everything that was done for labour should be done equally for the farmer.
The Liberal members of parliament were responsible for the fixed minimum price for wheat.
And that was so. There was no fixed minimum price in the original wheat board bill. I do not want to disparage what the right hon. leader of the opposition did. He was the father of the bill, very much approved by the godfather, the present Prime Minister, who amended it, and incidentally crucified it later by his government.
Mr. Bennett did not propose this when he brought in his wheat board bill. Mr. Bennett could have settled the wheat question earlier had he not wanted to make an election issue, but there was no issue as the bill received the support of all parties.
If that is the description of that bill- and it was a true description-I think I have to absolve my right hon. friend the then Prime Minister of Canada from wanting to make an issue of it. He wrestled with himself there that last day in 1935-oh, it was like dragging a cat by the tail to get him to do what he did. play the game; but he did play it. And he got a bill that committed this house, unanimously supported- even by Colonel Ralston-and if the government wanted harmony at this critical time surely it was not by murdering this bill in this horrible fashion that this desired end would be attained. I have pleaded with the government on this thing for the last two years, but they would not listen. Now I am forced to do what I am doing. I have been asked since the luncheon recess when I would be through. I do not know. "Well, don't you know that his excellency is going to sail on Monday?" I haven't anything to do with when his excellency sails. Let him sail. My duty is to my constituents and to the people of Canada; and without any disrespect whatever, and although I would love to meet the wishes of his excellency, it shall not be at the expense or neglect of the people of Canada or of my constituents.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission

speechtext:
May I say to
my hon. friend that I do not think his excellency's name should be brought into this discussion. As regards influencing the proceedings of parliament, no desire was expressed by his excellency with respect to his sailing or not sailing, nor was a word said by myself to the hon. member or to anyone else in regard to his speaking.

Yes, you wanted
to get that into Hansard, did you?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I wanted
to have the record correct.

Well I cannot hear what the hon. gentleman says. There was a colleague who lent me his ears the other day, but he and many others are not here to-day. Hon. members can guess why.
Now I have some simple notes here, but I never could follow notes. I am just going to follow the gleam. Here is the wheat board act. There were two little touches put to it by the senate afterwards, but they do not amount to a hill of beans, so we can take this as the act. I have it all marked and I know where to turn to anything; however it is getting so nearly worn out that it is not as easy as I thought. Here on the back of it are the notes I took at one meeting of mine in 1935. Here we have bill 98. passed in 1935, which in section 3 declares:
There shall be a board-
There was no "if" or "but" about it.
-to be known as The Canadian Wheat Board, which shall consist of three members appointed by the governor in council.
There are a good many important things in this bill, but these are the salient features:
7. The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat in interprovincial and export trade and for such purposes shall have all the powers of a corporation and without limitation upon such powers the following:
Surely anybody can understand that. You do not need to be an expert; you do not need to be the Minister of Justice. You hardly need to know anything at all to know what that means. Then it goes on;
(a)	to receive and take delivery of wheat for marketing as offered by the producers thereof;
(b)	to buy and sell wheat: Provided that no wheat shall be purchased by the board except from the producers thereof;
Is that not plain enough? If words mean anything at all, that board should have functioned continuously until parliament said no; not until somebody in the cabinet said no. I am sorry I was brought up such a stubborn Liberal, with the conceptions I have about democracy.
You were brought up in Lanark.

I see the hon. member for Lanark smiling. I am not providing this entertainment for my hon. friend; it is at a heavy cost to me. I remember my father talking about William Lyon Mackenzie, that great- man who challenged everything that was wrong at that time, including, to use his historian's very words, " the abuse of executive power." What a come-down that his grandson should exercise himself in the direction of abuse, great abuse, of executive .power. It is time this tendency to fascism was stopped. You do not need to go to Montreal for communists and that kind of truck. I suppose I should not have said "truck," but what I have said I have said. I tell you, when you get a government interfering in such an important matter as this, then you have a grave abuse of executive power and we must see that we get rid of that abuse. We must get rid of it, or how can we talk about unity? Is this not the way to get disunity? I suppose we should get a little practice against the Mussolini men, against fascists, before we have to go to a real war, but we do not want to start it here. If we do not we had better beware what we do.
I am not going to read the rest of this bill; it is so plain that "a wayfaring man, though he be a fool, need not err therein." Then, as though to make sure there would be no doubt about it, look at (g):
. . . generally to do all such other acts and things as may be necessary for the purpose of giving effect to the intent and meaning of this act.
Mark that. That was just for fear some of us were too stupid .to understand that the intent and meaning must be the guiding principle of the government that administered this measure. Is there anyone within sound of my voice who thought this bill could be crucified after a few months by an order in council? During the discussions in committee or elsewhere did anyone suggest, "Oh, well, the government can slip over an order in council"? Will anybody who thought that was in anybody's mind please stand up now and let us see what he looks like? No one stands up; then none have I offended.
Now let us go further:
8. It shall be the duty of the board:
(a)	to fix a price to be paid to the producers for wheat delivered to the board as by this act provided, subject to the approval of the governor in council;
(b)	to sell and dispose of from time to time all wheat which the board may acquire, for such price as it may consider reasonable, with the object of promoting the sale and use of Canadian wheat in world markets;

Supply

Trade-Grain Commission
Oh, I think you know it all, but down in (j) I find this:
. . . to offer continuously wheat for sale in the markets of the world through the established channels: Provided that the board may, if in its opinion any existing agencies are not operating satisfactorily, take such steps as it deems expedient to establish, utilize and employ its own or other marketing agencies or channels;
I am sure the right hon. leader of the opposition will correct me if I am wrong when I interpret that to mean that it was put in to see that no one else ever held wheat off the market in the same manner that it was thought to have been held off by the pool and the grain trade generally in the fall of 1929. Who will say that they did not all hold it off? And I never heard a soul say at that time they were wrong. They just guessed wrong; that was all. This provision, I take it, is put in to make sure that whoever is administering .this act will always remain in the market with their wheat, both buying and selling. I do not hear the leader of the opposition challenge that interpretation. I know that is what this provision was put in for. As I say, I was outside the committee, but I was constantly advised as to what was going on, and I helped a little bit at long range.
There are three provisions for the exercise of executive power in this bill. Sections 9, 10 and 11 provide for a compulsory wheat board if any government in power wants to have one. That power is granted in the bill. They also have the right to approve of a price for wheat as recommended by the board, or to modify that price. But the modification of the price was always thought to mean up or down, not laterally, as was done. Then there is another executive power found in section 14:
The governor in council may approve of the provisions of this act being made applicable to oats, barley, rye or flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if the board recommends that such approval be given, whereupon the provisions of this act shall mutatis mutandis-
Whatever that means; I think it means "in the same manner." They might just as well have said so, but the lawyers always like to put in something classical.
-apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
That power in two instances out of three has not been exercised. Well, when this parliament defined three executive powers that could be exercised, am I not justified in coming to the conclusion that this was all they were supposed to exercise? If they were meant to
kill the bill by stealth, parliament would have told them to steal up on it some dark night and put it out of business, but there is nothing like that here. I do not think there is anything like that in any act, but that is what has been done, while only one of these three provisions for the exercise of executive power has been taken advantage of, but with a bad twist in it.
There is the wheat board bill. I cannot imagine this order in council of the 90 cents a bushel racket being passed in total disregard of the plain language of that act, without its being referred to the Minister of Justice. I do not see him in his seat. I guess he is busy with the padlock law, and with those gentry away up near the foothills. But I do not see why he should confine his attention to them. Let him come here and give his reasons, which he must have given to his colleagues. I was in council long enough to know the procedure. If a minister of justice were passed up by the government you would soon be minus a minister of justice. No doubt the Minister of Justice passed upon this order in council. I do not know that he did; it may be that the rest of the cabinet turned around and did it without him. But they did not formerly do it in that way, in my day.
I will talk through you, Mr. Chairman, to my good old eastern Liberal friends. I was bom in Ontario, and I could not help loving it, even if I tried not to. It is pretty hard to ride through it these June days and see the beauties of its landscape without loving it, even if one were not born here. I have the affiliations. the attractions of birth place, the traditions, the memories of neighbours, and the story of old Ontario dating back to the early eighties and far beyond engraved clearly on my heart. But, oh, it makes me feel sad when I realize the way some of my eastern friends look at this matter. "If we have a wheat board for the west, everyone will be wanting a wheat board'-a board for onions, potatoes, cabbages, cheese and butter, etc. They will be clamouring from the Atlantic to the Pacific for boards, the same as the prairie farmers have."
That sounds logical and natural, superficially. That is the argument the Minister of Justice used on the second reading of the wheat board bill. I have too much truck on my desk to keep track of it. Read Hansard and see this, Messrs. Ministers, for yourselves! He spoke along those lines; I may not have the exact farm products mentioned, but that was the sense of it. That is the reason given why he wanted an emergent and very temporary board,-because everyone would be wanting one.
Now, let me answer that. During the war there were only two farm products which were

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
held down in price by the authorities of that day. One of them was wheat and the other was cheese. Those prices were held down officially. The price of cheese was held down to twenty-five cents a pound when there was no question that it would have soared sky high beyond that. I would say to members from the east:	Instead of shutting up your hearts
against the wheat board, which is admittedly for the west, why not claim your right for a cheese or live stock board? As I have said, during the great war you made sacrifices when the price of cheese was held down. Why not do now as I am doing? Why not claim the right to a board either for your cheese as an animal product, or for the animals themselves? That could easily be adjusted. Instead of wounding us in the west who in all conscience, need this in our business, why not claim your right, for reasons I shall show in a minute, to some assistance in the live stock industry or the live stock products industry, whichever you like?
That is a matter for yourselves. May I remind the government, and all members assembled here, that when the attempt was made to take the Crowsnest Pass rates from the west I pleaded with some of my maritime friends who are not here to-day that instead of trying to take that rate from us, something which had been obtained honestly and deliberately from Sir Wilfrid Laurier, they should get a little Crowsnest rate for the maritime provinces themselves. That is the way to do it, as I see it. If we are to live happily together it will be done not by snatching what the other fellow has, but by claiming the privilege of something similar on the principle of compensating adjustments for some other part of Canada. We cannot raise a family in this or any country without practising some give and take in order to promote peace within that family. That is what we must do if we are to promote peace and harmony among the nine provinces of this confederated country.
Well, they got their little Crowsnest railway rate in the maritimes, via the Duncan report route, and I think they were pretty happy about it. That would be my solution. Now, what did we contribute in the west to the bread-basket of the allies during the war? I do not know the facts with respect to cheese, because I never followed them up, and of course the figures would not reach such immense proportions as ours. But I have in my hand an extract from the proceedings of the royal grain inquiry, and I must give it credit where it is due for having brought out this fact. The information I have was sent to me, upon applica-
tion, by Mr. T. W. Grindley, when I asked him to give me something I could use respecting the prices of wheat under the board of grain supervisors. I have not used this information in any public meetings, because I have not been in the best of shape recently. When one spends nearly forty years of one's lile fighting for just such things as I am fighting for to-day, it grinds the stamina down pretty much. I became sick in 1829 on account of it; but I do not want sympathy on that account from anybody. I merely recite the fact for those not in the know. However I cannot help-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but

I want no mercy
at all. But do you think it is all right for the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) to speak at such great length? I will stop right here.
Go on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are in
committee, and if the hon. member will permit me I should hope he would regard these few words as giving him the opportunity to continue.
And I join in that.

That is nice. I
was not going to ask for it, because I am just not in the asking-for-favours-
Mood.

Yes, mood. But
you might as well let me have it off, anyway, because it is going to come off.

He knows he can do
it, anyway.

This is one
time that the private members have a chance;
I hope more of them will exercise it. I have before me an extract from page 762 of the evidence given on December 8, 1936. I find on looking over it the heading "Price limit," and following that heading this paragraph:
Above all, national selling held the price steady-
This was a reference to the board of grain commissioners.
-under conditions when, had there been no price control, the price would have been forced to an intolerable figure.
Yes, it would have been forced to an intolerable figure. Then Mr. Brockingtoa, counsel for the elevator association, asked:
I take it that means that the price would have been forced upward to an intolerable figure ?

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
Here is Mr. Ralston's statement:
I think that is what is meant there in the report of the board. In other words, national selling did effect a price limit. It held the price steady when, had there been no price control, the price would have been forced to an intolerable figure.
That is not what Colonel Ralston, said in Regina hearings or elsewhere. I think I am justified in saying that I was so ill when giving evidence at Regina that I could not proofread my own statement, and it never was proofread. I would not recommend anyone to read what I said. As everyone knows, it is very difficult to take down a grain letter correctly, but it appeared to be particularly hard in this case. Colonel Ralston talked me out of the vast sum the western farmers contributed during the war, owing to held down prices, when I was giving evidence before him. There is the record. I have a copy in my office, and any hon. member can get a copy. He talked me out of it. But if I had had the following information then, I would have taken the fur off the colonel.	I did enter into an altercation
with him of which I was ashamed. That happened before the press and everyone else. I am not going to bottle up the information that I have until it ferments.
The average fixed price paid for wheat in 1916, 1917 and 1918 worked out at about $2.28 per bushel. Very little was purchased in 1916, but for convenience of estimation we will place the average price at S2.28. When you are dealing in hundreds of millions of bushels it does not make much difference. Here is another significant item. It states that about 350,000,000 bushels were sold in those years by the board of grain supervisors, for which the farmers got an approximate average of $2.28 per bushel. Put that figure down in your scribbling books. Many estimates have been made as to what the price would have gone to if there had been no board. It is stated here that it would have gone to an "intolerable" height. What is an intolerable height? It went as high as $4 at the Atlantic seaboard, which is about 12 cents per bushel more than at Fort William. Let anyone look up the press of that day and he will find that the farmers and others were prophesying that wheat would go to $5. However, the authorities got together and held the price down to an average of $2.28. I have here an estimate made by about as capable a man as anyone I know in that line of business, the late Dr. Magill. He was the secretary of the Winnipeg grain exchange, an authority whom I do not often quote. The following statement appears on page 197 of the proceedings of the
committee on agriculture and colonization which met in 1922:
We bad no information about the British buying, and I stated that if the United States and Great Britain were going to compete in our market for our hard red fife it would not surprise me to see our wheat anywhere from $3 to $5 per bushel.
It must be remembered that that statement was made under oath. I think that is as sound an authority as you can find. I have no doubt the price would have gone that high. A middle figure between $3 and $5 would be $4. By deducting $2.28 from $4 you arrive at the extra amount the farmers would have received had there been no board. That gives you $1.72 per bushel. Multiply that by 350,000,000 bushels sold, and you get a total of nearly $600,000,000. That is the amount the farmers of the west contributed to the breadbasket of the allies including Canada. I will not say they all knew what was going on, but I do say there was very little murmuring about making that contribution. The average price of $2.28 looked like a lot of money. I do not want to magnify this too much. There are the figures and there is my authority. When I put the top price at $4 I am down a little from what it actually might have been. There was great difficulty in obtaining wheat at that time from the Argentine and Russia which forced the allies to depend almost entirely upon North America for their supply. If there had been no control the price might have gone higher than any of these estimates, but it was held down.
Have you ever noticed how prompt governments are to act when they want to hold down farm prices? Without any prodding, without any urging, without any goad being used, they jump to keep prices down. That is what happened in connection with the wheat at that time, 1916, 1917 and 1918. When you want governments to hold up prices even a wee bit, when you want them to give you a wheat board, how reluctant they are to act I Reluctant is hardly the word to use; how determined they are not to do itl We hear a lot about the hardships of the farmers and the beneficence of governments in the matter of relief seed, etc. That will not do for me. I will not sell my independence even though I am fed, or even though my neighbours are fed. It may be all right to keep them alive like you would an ox so that you can get some work out of them, but that is not Christianity, it is not even decent. I appeal to this government, to my old companions and friends, not to continue snatching wheat boards from us by peculiar orders in council, but to go forward and do something Do not wait for weeks to pass before it is

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
put into effect. This order in council referred to was passed on August 27, 1936, twenty-seven days after it should have been passed as provided by law and then was no good. This is the time-almost the first of July-to set the price for the coming harvest. It should be set at 87i cents basis Fort William, with no cussed rider to it such as burdened the orders in council of two years ago and last year. Is it done? Will it be done? The answer was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that in addition to what the Turgeon commission reported favourably on, we would have a board and a minimum fixed price. There was nothing in the Turgeon commission report, except by implication, that there would be a fixed minimum price. You have to read closely between the lines to see even that, so closely that the Minister of Trade and Commerce relieved the anxiety of the western people by telling them that there would be a fixed minimum price. Do you think that I have not now the right to urge that price? When is the minister going to set the price? If he uses the board and the people out west the way that they have been used since the 27th of August, 1936, what kind of price are we going to get? Are we as representatives going to disband from this house and run the chance of similar treatment this fall? Once bitten, not twice shy, but many more times shy. Do you think we should trust the government to do the right thing, not on the 27th of August, but now, or say a week from now, when we and they get away? Do you think we should complacently trust them after what they did in 1936? If you think that, then "I have not found so great faith, no not in Israel." They should not ask us to go abroad and take it for granted that they are going to do something in the way of a price which will be in any wise acceptable to the people. Why strain our confidence in that way ? Why not " come across"? Why do not the government adopt the recommendation of the wheat sub-committee? I do not think it is any breach of confidence- if anyone thinks it is I will not say what I intend to say-to mention that this was not in council. The subcommittee of the government-four gentlemen, all capable men-met one from Alberta and the Liberal members from Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and without one dissenting voice the subcommittee was asked for a board and for a price such as I have suggested, and we wanted it before this house prorogued. They-the sub-committee were not very anxious about acquiescing in that request, but after they had reported to the cabinet they came back and seemed quite agreeable.
FMr. Motherwell.]
Came back where?

But that is as far as it has gone. It would look as though the ones who are most responsible are the remaining members of the cabinet other than the four members of the subcommittee. I cannot get at the bottom of that. I do not think we are going to be flim-flammed by that kind of treatment. The subcommittee will get away with it on the ground that they made a recommendation to full council, and the rest of them will get away with it in any way they can. They will be down here, anyway, where little sentiment for wheat boards prevails, so it will not make much difference to them politically. If I am exaggerating or going farther than I should, let anyone who likes cast a stone.
I have been identified with the subject-matter of this legislation since its inception and even during its pre-natal stage,-when the late Doctor Douglas introduced the matter in a private bill in 1898, and for ten years before that. I do not like to obtrude the "I"

that "I" did this and the other. You can imagine what I was like in those days, forty years younger than I am now. You may be sure that I was somewhere around when this Manitoba grain act subject was first discussed. We made' pretty good progress until 1912-I will not say until the Tories came in, though things just happened that way, but the Tories were not a bit worse than we have been since. Then that precious sample market business was ingeniously worked into the picture, and the farmers bit like so many pikes-hungry ones too. To their astonishment they found that wheat grade mixing was ingeniously worked in at the request of Doctor Magill to the Minister of Trade and Commerce of that day; that is 1917. Anyone who wishes can look at the records; I have not them here. That was done through a minister of trade and commerce-I hope he is listening to this-
He is in heaven.

I mean the present Minister of Trade and Commerce-who interviewed the Minister of Justice and got a decision that authority for a sample market presupposed mixing. What the grain trade cannot do when it comes to driving through the Grain Act is not worth talking about. But I must not dwell too long on that. I may mention what the farmers contributed-if you like, what they sacrificed-at that time to the cause of the allies. Will you not now let us check out a little bit on that credit-

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
not the stuff that is talked about up in the country of high altitudes; this credit of ours is a real credit-
So is ours,

-so that we may get through this crisis without being told daily that we are "bumming" on eastern Canada. I admit that eastern Canada is helping us generously. We have been helped by both church and state, and we acknowledge it freely, but we are not selling our birthright because of that, or our conceptions of what is proper in these matters.
How would it be, Mr. Chairman, if we should now take recess? There is too much ammunition here to keep track of; my desk is full of it; hon. members want to prorogue; his excellency wants to sail; what am I going to do? I am going to stand by with this ammunition as long as I can stand up and deliver. I am going to call it half time with the hope and expectation of delivering the remainder of it some time to-day.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
It is not my intention to follow
into all the by-ways traversed by the two
previous speakers.
In the opening remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) I was surprised to hear him intimate that the appointment of the Turgeon commission was not the result of the meeting of our parliamentary committee or of anything that was said in this house with regard to certain charges against Mr. Murray. His further criticism was that there has not been sufficient time for the discussion of the wheat board and its activities. As hon. members know, the report was laid on the table the very day after Mr. Justice Turgeon delivered the first report to me; it was laid on the table even before it was printed. The printed report was laid on the table within two weeks afterwards. Therefore, at least so far as the government is concerned, there was no delay in presenting the report to members of the house. That it is not possible perhaps to give it full consideration is not the fault of the government, and it is because of the importance of the recommendations that are made in the report that the government finally decided not to bring in this session any legislation that would implement some of the recommendations made by the commissioner. There may be, and there has been, some criticism with regard to that, but I would ask the committee to accept it as the reason. It had been the intention of the government to bring in legislation amending the grain act to provide for supervision of the Winnipeg grain ex-51952-282
change; but, as I said before, for the reason that, the house being in session, we were not able to give the question full consideration, we finally decided, rightly or wrongly, that the whole matter should be left over until next session. Then possibly there will be a complete revision of the grain act, and whatever may arise out of the report may be incorporated in that act.
The hon, member for Qu'Appelle complained about the length of time taken by the commissioner in the investigation and the submission of the report. He made a comparison between Judge Turgeon and Sir Josiah Stamp. No proper comparison is possible, because, if I remember rightly, Sir Josiah Stamp reported on just one question, that dealing with futures on the Winnipeg grain exchange, and that required only a few weeks. The order of reference to Judge Turgeon was vastly wider than that. Not only did it necessitate inquiries in Winnipeg and in every grain centre in the west, but the commissioner had to proceed to Europe and Great Britain, and as a natural consequence the report was delayed. I might give as another reason, though it may not be accepted as a good one, the fact that Judge Turgeon was the commissioner in charge of the investigation into the textile industry. For those reasons the grain report was somewhat delayed.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle dealt with three or four definite points. In the first place he criticized the delay in bringing in the report, and second-I am not using language that is too strong-his criticism was a defamation of three estimable gentlemen who have served the country well. One of these gentlemen is Colonel Ralston, who, the committee will admit, was one of the most valuable and reputable members of this house. Another was Mr. Murray, former chairman of the wheat board. The hon. member also criticized Mr. Mclvor, the present chairman of the wheat board, a man who was associated with Mr. McFarland, and I believe my hon. friend had a great deal of confidence in Mr. McFarland whose name he mentioned to-day. He used these terms, which I took down, and he will correct me if I am wrong. I believe his reference to Mr. Murray was as a criminal, and he referred to Mr. Mclvor as an accomplice in crime.
That is figurative language, and the hon. gentleman knows it.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend say that. In another instance he spoke of the hangman. I leave it to the judgment of the committee whether that is



Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
proper language to use, even in jest, of any reputable men who have served the country well. I was going to use strong terms in condemning the bon. member's language-
Why does the minister not address bis remarks to the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell)? He spoke more disparagingly of Mr. Ralston.

I am not at the moment replying to the hon. member for Melville. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle made reference to men who are not in this house to defend themselves, and I say to him that if he puts himself in a position where they can defend themselves, they will take very good care of him. The other point of his speech was a criticism of the report itself, and finally he gave advice to the government as to the policy that should be pursued in connection with the wheat board for the coming crop year.
I am not going to go into all the ramifications of the charges made. The original charges against Mr. Murray as chairman of the wheat board were made in this chamber, as a result of which a parliamentary committee was appointed, of which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) were members. I happened to be the chairman of that committee. These charges were investigated by that committee; the report which was made to this house was unanimous, and certainly there was in the report no condemnation of Mr. Murray or anyone else.
It did not exonerate him at all.

In the report the recommendation was made that a royal commission should be appointed to look into the matter of these charges, and of the whole question of wheat and the policy with regard to wheat. Judge Turgeon was appointed as royal commissioner; he made his investigations, and I need only say in regard to the charges made in that committee that the house can do nothing other than accept the report of the commissioner, with regard to the charges against Mr. Murray, that he had protected the shorts on a certain day; I believe it was in December, 1935. I will read one paragraph from the commissioner's report:
In answer to the question arising out of paragraph 3 of the order in council, I find, on the whole of the evidence that the members of the board cannot be said to have protected speculative short interests in the Winnipeg wheat market in December, 1935. The board, in the exercise of its legitimate discretion, decided that it was advisable to sell. They sold without, of course, knowing what propor-

tion of their sales would fall to speculators and what proportion to others: and I cannot see how a knowledge that short speculators were buying should have deterred them from selling, if they had such knowledge.
This being my opinion, the second question as to the effect of any such protection does not call for an answer.
How many witnesses were called to prove that?
I was not present and I do not know how many witnesses were called, but there is the fact that the commissioner reports that no blame rests upon Mr. Murray.
It is not denied that they were protected by what took place; but the *commissioner says that they did not intend to do it.
It is true the result might have been to the advantage of speculators, but it is an entirely different thing to say that the action of the chairman of the board was calculated to protect the shorts.
Every man is supposed to know the effects of his own acts.

Absolutely not. My right hon. friend might buy wheat to-day, thinking there would be an increase in price, and yet it might go down. The hon. member also described Mr. Murray as a dictator, and I refer to that particularly because, knowing Mr. Murray as I do, I consider it was a most unjust attack. It was intended also to be a reflection upon the government, that he dictated to the government.
So he did. He said he must hire his own people, and you remember what he said about taking office at all.
The action taken with respect to the advisory committee was due to the policy of the government and not to the desire of Mr. Murray.
What about Murray's evidence at page 191?

The hon. member made
another statement, that there was a fire sale; that after McFarland retired from the board and Murray took charge, a fire sale was put on to the detriment of the wheat producers. I say distinctly that the policy which was adopted by the wheat board of offering wheat for sale at all times was not only what was called for very definitely in the wheat board act, put through this house by the then government, led by the present leader of the opposition, but was the considered policy of this government. We believed that this was the right policy to follow. I admit that there

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
is room for difference of opinion on that. No doubt my hon. friends on the other side believe that the policy followed by Mr. McFarland in accumulating almost 300 million bushels of wheat and keeping the whole wheat situation in a state of uncertainty may have been the right one. But this government thought otherwise, and Mr. Murray in offering wheat for sale at all times followed definitely the policy and desire of this government, with the result that we got rid of the wheat surplus.

And lost $11,000,000 on
his operations.
But at one time we would have lost about $75,000,000 if we had followed the policy of my right hon. friend.
But the answer is he did not, and he made $25,000,000 out of McFarland's wheat.

The agreement was made without the knowledge of the government and was cancelled without the knowledge of the government the moment Murray met with the committee of the grain exchange. That is the evidence.
I do not know whether such an agreement ever was made.

Last year I asked for the return, showing whether the government knew of that agreement, and the answer was: No. I asked a second question: Did they know when it was cancelled? And it was cancelled without the authority of the government and was made without their authority.

Quite right, and in the
language of the street, "So what?'' Certainly the government did not dictate to Mr. Murray in regard to any of his acts. But Mr. Murray, generally speaking, was carrying out the policy of this government in offering wheat for sale at all times.
Read these documents.
And that is also the law laid down in the wheat board act.
He has done a number of things the government did not know.

The hon. member for
Qu'Appelle criticises the recommendations made by Judge Turgeon. That, of course, is his privilege. One recommendation was that there should be legislation to provide for the supervision of the grain exchange at Winnipeg. I was a little surprised when my hon. friend read a great many opinions, including 51952-2824
that of Mr. McFarland by the way, and, I think, of Mr. Murray and a good many others, that the Winnipeg grain exchange should be supervised. But he followed that up with a statement, or certainly the implication, that the grain exchange ought to be abolished altogether. I do not see the consistency of the two statements. I do not know what my hon. friend wants. Does he want the grain exchange supervised or abolished?
I said the grain exchange in the open market could continue with a board but under proper supervision.

I am afraid I misunderstood my hon. friend.
Another suggestion made by the commissioner is that wheat should be sold through the pools, and that the government should encourage the organization of pools to handle the sale of wheat, and, he said in so many words that ultimately he believed the government should get out of the wheat business altogether. With that I entirely agree. He also said that for the coming year-it was more or less a negative recommendation-the wheat board might continue. That answers the question my hon. friend asked this morning, or what I am going to say will answer it and also answer the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). As a result of that recommendation the government announced some weeks ago through myself that there would be a wheat board to handle the crop for the coming crop year and that a price would be set at an appropriate date.
And participating certificates issued?

That is what the law
requires.

I think it is utterly impossible under the wheat board act to set a price without participation; I think that naturally follows. What that price may be, I am not prepared to state, because the government had not considered that question. That will be done in due course.
There was another recommendation which at the moment I do not regard as of great importance, that there should be a wheat institute to promote the sale of wheat in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe. In regard to that the wheat board itself, in the last year and the year preceding, has been doing that work. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition intimated that he thought they were spending that ;money illegally. I am not in a position at the moment to say anything as to that except

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
that it never occurred to me that they had not a perfect right to do anything they could to promote the sale of wheat, which it was their job to sell. Now that the wheat board is going to continue for the coming crop year, there is no doubt at all, because I spoke to the chairman about it, that he will continue those efforts to promote the sale of wheat both in Great Britain and on the continent.
In conclusion, just a word in regard to the demands of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. He demanded that we promise him, I suppose, or the house, certain things.
The farmers of western Canada.

That we promise that we would have a wheat board with a fixed price and with participation, knowing all the time that the government had already stated their intention to do that very thing. But I suppose that would read well in the headlines.
I have not any more confidence in the government than has the hon. member for Melville.

I would not expect my hon. friend to have much confidence in anything. And as someone over here says, it is the first time he has ever followed the hon. member for Melville. He will probably follow him only when he feels in sympathy with him.
He did not follow the hon. member for Melville, the hon. member for Melville followed him.

Well, probably the two hon. gentlemen will follow each other; perhaps they are good mates. He also demanded that we declare the full policy of the government with regard to wheat board matters. He demands a price of 874 cents. Here he and his mate are not quite in agreement; the hon. member for Melville was satisfied with 85 cents. They will have to get together and decide what they want.
As to what the price is going to be, I am not making any promise, for the simple reason that the government has not yet decided what that price shall be. In due course the price will be announced.
I do not know that I can say anything more in regard to policy. It seems to me that nothing more should, at this time, be demanded of the government by the committee. The committee is assured; the farmers of western Canada are assured, that there is going to be a wheat board operating during the coming crop year. They are assured that there will be a fixed minimum

price. They are assured that there will be participation, because there must be if the wheat board act is continued.
The act is not repealed or amended.
Quite so; that is why I say that. If we had intended to do away with participation, it would be necessary to amend the wheat board act, and we have no such intention.
No; you did it by order in council the last two years. That is the point.
In conclusion, the policy of the government for the coming year with regard to the wheat board act is as I have stated it, pending decision during the coming year as to a permanent policy.

I wish to make a few brief comments. First, I would refer to the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). I have often found myself in disagreement with him. Indeed, on more than one occasion ideas which I hold have been subjected to his ridicule. But I realize that it took a great deal of courage to do what he did this afternoon, after so many years in this house, with so many associations with his party, to rise in his place and criticise the government and inferentially the party of which he has been so long-I say it quite sincerely-a distinguished member. This afternoon the hon. member for Melville answered something that I think we found it rather difficult to answer; that is, the suggestion that the agitation in the fall of 1936 against the government's action in connection with the wheat board was the result of political opposition to the government and particularly of the activity of some of us connected with this group. I think the former Minister of Agriculture demonstrated clearly this afternoon that this dissatisfaction not only was felt by people politically opposed to the party represented by the government but was widespread in the ranks of all parties, and included government supporters in western Canada. I was glad to hear the announcement made this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler).
That was nothing new.

We were anxious to know definitely that there would be a wheat board; that it would operate continuously; that there would be a set minimum price, and that there would be participation certificates

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
during the coming year. I think that announcement made so categorically this afternoon will be welcomed generally.
Does my hon. friend not know that I made the same announcement some three weeks ago? Perhaps my hon. friend was away in Saskatchewan at that time.

I did not realize that it was made quite so specifically. In common with a number of gentlemen supporting the minister I was, as he says, away in Saskatchewan when he made that announcement in the house. But it having been made this afternoon in this manner, I think it is much more satisfactory than I realized from the previous announcement.
With regard to the minimum price, I am in agreement with the hon. member for Melville when he says that our producers are entitled to minimum prices for their products. As I have said so frequently in the house, if our producers must buy in a protected market then the prices they get ought to be protected also; and from the votes taken in the house on the budget and the subamendment a short time ago, I think we may take it for granted that the government intends to maintain at least a certain amount of tariff protection. With regard to the set price, the minister stated that two previous speakers who had mentioned fixed prices had differed in the price suggested, but at the risk of making confusion worse confounded I am going to differ also and suggest to the minister that the proper way to fix a price is to take the results of investigations which have been made into the costs of production over a period of years. If the government will do that, I think they will find that the university of Saskatchewan has made fairly exhaustive studies of average prices and has stated rightly or wrongly-I believe rightly- that the cost of producing and delivering a bushel of wheat at Fort William amounts on the average, to $1.03, which is the figure suggested by Professors Allan and Hope of that university. Therefore, I say our producers are entitled to that consideration.
There is not much left for me to say after the announcement of the minister and particularly after the speeches of the hon. member for Melville and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), but we shall hope that when the permanent policy is brought down it will place in statutory form, that cannot and will not be upset by government orders in council, a fair and just price for the western producer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no desire to take up any of the time of the committee with reference to the general discussion which has taken place, but I do wish to deal immediately and precisely with the allegation that in passing the order in council that has been the subject of discussion this afternoon the government believed in any way whatever that it was nullifying in any particular any provision of the wheat board act. From what the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has said, one would assume that the government had deliberately sought to undermine the effect of an act which had been passed by this parliament, that we had tried to do by order in council what the statute would not permit us to do.
Two questions came up for consideration at the time the matter was being discussed in council. The first was that of the legal power of the government to take action along the lines it did. In connection with that aspect of the matter legal advice was taken by the government from the Department of Justice, and from the advice given us I was perfectly satisfied at the time, as I believe all my colleagues were, that under the provisions of the act we had authority to pass the order in council we did.
The other question that came up for consideration was whether or not our action in naming the price to which wheat would have to fall before it would be purchased by the board would meet with the approval of the wheat board itself. The wheat board was consulted before the figure of 90 cents was finally agreed to by the governor in council, and they approved it. The order in council was not passed, as I have said, until after we had reason to believe that we had full legal authority for what we were doing and also until we believed we were acting in accordance with what the wheat board itself considered to be the wise and right thing to do. There may be debate as to whether or not our judgment in the matter was right or wrong. I submit, however, that the record of prices from the time the order in council was passed up to the present shows pretty conclusively that our judgment was sound in the course we took. With respect to the powers we had, I think I have only to read the sections of the act that are pertinent and leave it to hon. gentlemen who wish to take a fair and unbiased view of the situation to say whether or not we were in their opinion justified in the view we entertained as to our powers under the act. Section 7 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, which refers to the powers of the board, is as follows:
On what authority did he dismiss the advisory committee for which there is provision in the act?
It says only that there may be an advisory committee.
An advisory committee had been set up.
It was not obligatory.
It was set up, though.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot answer the question, because I have not that information in my mind at the moment.

I am not a lawyer, but I would say it would naturally follow that if it is within the authority of the government to set up a board or not to set up a board, then there surely ought to be power to nullify action which had been taken.
It does not say " may."

I rise to ask two questions, but before doing so may I express my admiration of the courage and fine independence of spirit indicated this afternoon by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). Those of us from Saskatchewan who know about the fight he has put up for cooperative marketing to the advantage of the farmers of that province know how well he has shown his integrity this afternoon by carrying his views to their logical conclusion. As I heard him speak, I could not help thinking of what Tennyson made Ulysses say:
You and I are old;
Old age hath yet his honour and his toil.
My only regret is that the great party to which the hon. member belongs could not see fit to keep pace with him.
The statement has been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and was made in Saskatchewan [DOT]repeatedly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), that there would be a wheat board. Are we, from that, to understand definitely that the operation of the Wheat board will not be contingent upon any price level? The Prime Minister pointed out a moment ago that constitutionally the government had the power to pass the order in council. I am not concerned with the constitutional aspect of the matter, but I am concerned with the fact that the effect of that order in council was to make the wheat board inoperative.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
The minister says we are going to have a wheat board. We have a wheat board, but it is a wheat board which .cannot take delivery of wheat until the price hits 90 cents. Are we to have that kind of wheat board, one which will operate only when the price hits a certain level? Will it be operative to-day and not operative to-morrow, operative this week and not operative next week? Is the minister prepared to assure us it will be a wheat board which will take delivery of wheat, irrespective of the price level? That is my first question.
My second question is this: Is the minister prepared to give us the assurance that a fixed minimum price will be announced within a reasonable period before wheat is being placed on the market by the producers? The farmers ought to know now what the fixed price is going to be. When I was in Saskatchewan a few weeks ago wheat was leaving the elevators as seed wheat, under a federal government guarantee, and farmers were signing notes for SI.45 a bushel. On the other hand wheat was going into the elevator at 72 cents a bushel. I was in a municipal office and saw a man signing a note for wheat which had been supplied to him by a mortgage company. That note was for wheat at the rate of $1.70 a bushel. That man will .probably bring back three bushels for every bushel he received from the mortgage company. If prices continue at the average present level, he will bring back two bushels of wheat for every bushel received.
I say the farmers have a right to expect that long before they are drawing their wheat to the elevators they will know something about what the price will be. I would, therefore, ask the minister these questions: First, will the operations of the wheat board be contingent upon the price level on a particular day and, second, will farmers be given notice, within a reasonable period of time before wheat is being put on the market, as to what the fixed minimum price for wheat will be this fall?

I have already stated the government has not yet considered what the price should be. I would add that nothing in connection with the fixing of that price, or any modifying or restrictive price, has been considered.
With respect to the second question as to whether or not a decision will be made within a reasonable time as to the fixing of a price, the answer is in the affirmative. I might add that the decision with respect to the first question will also be made within a reasonable time.

In order that I might not misunderstand may I ask this: Do I understand the minister is not prepared to give the assurance that there will not be the same danger as before of an inoperative clause which will say that until the price hits a certain level the wheat board will not take delivery?

I cannot give any assurance, because the matter has not been discussed or decided upon by the government. That is my reason for saying I cannot give an assurance. It is a matter of policy, and I am not authorized to make statements with regard to policy. The matter has not been decided upon.
In other words, when the minister says there will be a wheat board he means there will be a wheat board with qualifications.

No; I am not saying that at all. I am saying there will be a wheat board and a minimum price, and the other matter in connection with it, as to what the price shall be, is to be decided within a reasonable time. I think that is quite clear.
I must differ with the minister; I do not think it is clear. It is clear there will be a wheat board and a fixed minimum price, but it is not clear that the wheat board will accept delivery of wheat.
No; that is not decided. My answer with regard to it is clear, that there will be a decision within a reasonable time.
The minister said there would be participation certificates?
It is in the statute; he cannot help saying it.
Yes; it is statutory. But that is only if the board takes delivery.
Yes.

The inference which has been taken is this, that the participation certificate means that the farmer will be able to deliver to that board every day of the year, and will participate to the extent of the average price. That is the interpretation which has been and is being placed in western Canada upon the participation certificate. Now we learn that while it is statutory, there is no guarantee that the board will operate in the manner it is expected to operate by the farmers of the west.

It is statutory that if the board purchases wheat and sells it for a price higher than that at which it purchases, there will be participation.
No; when it buys it will give a participation certificate.

Yes, a participation certificate which will ensure that if the wheat is sold at a price higher than is paid for it, the producer will get the balance. Perhaps it may be difficult to satisfy all hon. members, but I do say that the decision with regard to price and everything connected with it will be made within a reasonable time.

falling?

to prevent the board from buying a bushel of wheat, and it succeeded. It was intended to permit the grain trade to monopolize the business, as they did. Not a single bushel of wheat was bought by the wheat board. That is the answer. It is no good to be righteously indignant about this. The fact is that not one bushel of wheat was bought. The grain trade monopolized the business that was intended to be divided between private and public concerns. Read the debates in this parliament. Read the story of the debate that brought this wheat board into being. The story was simple. It was that the farmers of western Canada should have an alternate market; they were to have the public market or the private market. They could go to the wheat board, on the one hand, or to the private interests, on the other. But they were denied the right to go to the public board; they were driven to

the private grain trade. Every bushel of wheat sold by the farmers of western Canada since the expiration of the crop year in which the government came into office has passed through private hands.
They got a good price.

The fact that they got a good price is not the answer. The answer is that they were deprived of their alternate market. There is another answer, which is a complete one. It is the one made by the bon. member for Melville-the farmers did not share in the profit.
They got the going price.

Yes; they got the going price, but the private interests made the profit that should have gone to the farmer under the participation certificates. That is the point exactly. That is the whole story. That is the point made to-day by the hon. member for Melville. He complains because this board has not functioned. It has not functioned because an order in council was passed that rendered it impossible for the board to function. It is admitted that this is so. There is no denial of it. The profit that went to the private interests is a profit that would have gone to the farmers of this country under the participation certificates. That is the whole story.
They did not do that the previous year.
No one says they did. I am talking about 1936-37 and 1937-38.
Does my right hon. friend say that there should have been a guarantee of a profit on the board's operations in 1936-37 when there might have been a loss as there was in 1935-36?

Surely the minister
realizes that no one is talking about guarantees.
My right hon. friend is talking about profits that were denied to the farmers.
Nobody was talking about guarantees. I want to make that clear to the minister.
There is no point in such a statement.
Yes.
There was no profit in 1935-36.
No. The farmers got 874 cents, and the country paid $11,000,000.
I understood my right hon. friend to say there would be a profit.

That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) has just said, that there was a profit. I say that profit did not go to the farmers of the country.
Mr. EUiLER: Does my right hon. friend think the theory of the act should be that there should be a profit guaranteed to the farmers by the Canadian government?

I have not suggested that. I am not talking about the theory of the act; I am talking about the operation of the act. I am pointing out to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) that there was a great profit last year, but it did not go to the farmers. They would have derived the benefits of that profit had there been participation certificates.
My right hon. friend has no warrant for making such a statement.
I say they would have participated in the profits.
They got the market price.

They got the market price at which the wheat was hauled in, in the fall, but that is not the price which the ultimate consumer paid. The best answer is that there is a spread of 25 cents. What price is the farmer paying at the elevator for the seed wheat the wheat board took over? Under what authority did they take it? The farmers of Saskatchewan are paying $1.45 a bushel. At what did they take it from the wheat board? They took it at $1.24. By what authority? For what was the profit of 20 cents a bushel? What authority had they to do that? That is the figure given to me by the minister. He is the one who said that the wheat board sold at $1.45.
The price that will be finally charged to the farmer has not yet been set.
The minister himself said that the price would be $1.45.
I have never made the statement that the price was set at $1.45. Read the record.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has said that the price has not been set, so that settles that. I was basing my argument on the statement that the price was $1.45. There is no getting away from the fact that this act was intended *to be for the benefit of the farmers of west-

ern Canada. They complained of tariffs and this was to be the compensating adjustment. They were told that if there was a loss, the country would bear it. But the fact is that not a bushel of wheat has passed into the possession of the wheat board for two years. Why? Because the government passed an order in council that made it impossible.

Because the government passed an order in council that said it would not operate until wheat fell to 90 cents. Let us have it referred to the Supreme Court of Canada.
