speechtext: That is not what was done here.

That is exactly what was done. There cannot be any difference of opinion about that because not a single bushel of wheat passed into the elevators for the wheat board in 1936-37; not one bushel- which is the test. I know farmers who went to elevators and were willing to take the risk. They said, "We will take a chance," and they wanted to give their thousand bushels of wheat to the wheat board. They were not concerned about the price. That was not a matter of importance. They wanted a participation certificate, to share in that rise in price. Could they do it? That is the test. Farmer A goes to-day to Okotoks with 1,000 bushels of wheat, as he did last fall, and asks to put it in the elevator for the wheat board. He cannot do so. Why? Because the price of wheat is not as low as 90 cents. He was willing to take the chance. He wanted the alternate market; he wanted a participation certificate; he wanted the opportunity, believing as he did that wheat was going to rise in price, to share in that rise. Could he do so?
What chance would he possibly be taking under those circumstances?
He was willing to take a chance by selling to the wheat board. He was bound then to get the very highest price at which the wheat was sold.

He was bound to get the
price at which it was ultimately sold. He was not taking a chance at all.
He would take a chance on making some money. He would take a chance of participating in a rising market.
Exactly. The chances were all in his favour.
Exactly.
He could not lose out, because the government would lose if the price went below 87i cents, and he must win if the price went above that. It was " Heads I win and tails you lose."
What is the difference between giving it to the farmer and giving it to the gambler?
That is not the point at all.

In one year seven billion bushels were handled in the Winnipeg grain exchange. Does the hon. gentleman mean to tell me that he can justify that? That one fact convinced me more than all other arguments together that we must have control. I ask every reasonable man in this house whether he does not agree, when he is confronted with the evidence that seven billion bushels of wheat were 'bought and sold on the market in Winnipeg in one year when the crop was hedged to the extent of less than two hundred million bushels, and when the total crop amounted to about three hundred and five million bushels. I ask, apart from partisan feeling and political differences, whether any member of this committee thinks that-kind of thing can be justified.
What did the Stamp commission say about it?
The Stamp commission said it should be supervised.
No; on the matter of speculation?

I may say that I wrote the question, because I was anxious to have the opinion upon it of that economist, a disinterested man. The simple question was whether or not the sale of futures was advantageous or otherwise to the farmer, and the answer was that it was, but that there should be supervision.
Was there? Was supervision provided for?
I will tell the hon. gentleman. In the wheat board act we had a provision that would enable us to wipe that practice out altogether.

When was the Stamp report brought in?

Not any.
Why?

Why? Because we were controlling the market. Against the efforts of those who are now the government, we were controlling the market. That is the reason. And that is the reason why the whole grain exchange was arrayed against the then government. I could, with respect to that, unfold a tale which would amuse the hon. gentleman. I know what I am talking about. I know what their efforts were. I know who conducted them. I know the contributions made to the end that the government should be destroyed. They were quite within their rights, because they thought they were fighting for their lives. That control was the reason it was not necessary to do more than make this adjustment. It is available also to pay the $15,000,000 which this country improperly paid, in order to make political capital, as a business man once said, probably the most discreditable operation that ever took place in parliament, in face of a written document which stated that payment should not be made until the ultimate liability was established. In the face of that, they paid it. Well, you add $6,000,000 and $15,000,000 and you get $21,000,000.
Do not forget the $11,000,000 loss in 1935.

I am not talking about that; I am talking about McFarland's operations. Here are the documents that show a surplus in these operations of $24,000,000, there being still adjustments to be made-a surplus which pays the $6,000,000 and the $15,000,000, leaving something towards the payment of the $11,000,000. I do not know how much that will be. When we get down to the 1935 operations, I have not time this evening to go over these documents; but they will be here, and if I am not here then, somebody else will be who will take these sales and analyse them. When you look at the sales for 1935 and 1936 you will understand why there was a loss. All you have to do is take the weekly reports. The law required them to offer wheat for sale, but if you analyze these reports you will know why the term "fire sale" is used. There is no trouble about that. Read the reports; I have read them all. I have seen the sales for June, 1935; I have seen the sales on single days, and I know exactly what is meant by the term. That is the reason why the discussion has taken place as to the benefits that accrued bo certain interests. It is all very well for the commissioner to say that they did not intend to do it, but there are the documents and they speak for themselves. I ask any hon. gentleman to take the reports, which are given for every week in the year commencing in 1935, before this government came into office, and coming down to June 18, 1938, and to read those reports. If you will read them you will understand why there was a surplus of $24,000,000 on one account and why there was a loss of $11,000,000 on the other; for remember that during the crop period they were not selling McFarland wheat; they were bound not to, as a matter of fact; Mr. Murray made that clear before the committee.
If one did justice to this subject, one would deal with it methodically and carefully from beginning to end; but I realize that we are now at the end of the session and I do not propose to do more than state the propositions which I have put forward, which do not admit of denial. A farmer who desired to use the alternate market, having 1,000 bushels of wheat last fall, and to get the participation certificate, taking his chance, was denied that right by the passing of an order in council which renders nugatory the provisions of the wheat board act in that regard. I will ask any student of law whether or not any body given power to impose conditions can impose a condition that renders nugatory the operation of the statute under which they are given that power. That is the issue, shortly put. It is put in other

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
words by a layman, the hon. member for Melville, but I put it in this way to members of the committee who belong to the legal profession, and who know that the foundation of all our liberty lies in the fact that it is not competent for any body, in the exercise of a power conferred upon it, to impose a condition which prevents the exercise of the power for which it was created. That is elementary, and it is for that reason that I have objected to the orders in council of 1935 and 1936. When the minister says to the committee that the wheat board is to be made operative; that there is to be a wheat board, I tell him that there is a wheat board now. The statute has not been amended or repealed since we passed it in July, 1935; it still stands, and it can be prevented from operating only by an act of this parliament.
The hon. member for Melville has pointed out that Colonel Ralston at that time, on behalf of the opposition, endeavoured to have an amendment passed by which the act would lapse automatically. We objected; we said no. We said that parliament should act; that the government has no longer to pass a wheat board act because there is one on the statute books,
That is quite conceded. I did not intend to give the impression that the government could refuse to allow the board to act without repealing or modifying the act.

We are at one there. There remains, then, but one thing to be done. The government should fix a price so as to express approval or disapproval of the recommendation made by the board, because the responsibility rests in the first place with the board. As I pointed out, away back in 1935 the board recommended a price far in excess of 874 cents, to which we would not agree, and finally after discussion and negotiation we reached 874 cents, which they recommended and the governor in council approved.
Very reluctantly.
The hon. gentleman was not a member of that administration.
I have heard it.

He has not heard it from anybody within the government. The price of 874 cents was approved because an effort was made to have a higher price, which the government did not regard as reasonable under the then existing conditions. The government now have to do only two things: one, to secure the recommendation of the board; two, to approve. They need not approve the recommendation if they do not regard it as
satisfactory, but they cannot impose a condition which prevents the board from operating, and be within the law; for every farmer has a right to that alternate market which the order in council has denied him; and if he was willing to take his chance, waiting until the crop year ended, that he might have the value of his participation certificate determined, he should have been permitted so to do. The government prevented him from doing that. That is common ground, and it is for that reason I have suggested that the validity of the order in council should be referred to the supreme court. It cannot be litigated, but it should be referred to the supreme court, the simple question being: Can an order in council be passed that renders it impossible for a farmer to sell his wheat to the wheat board? That is the only question. This order in council prevents him from doing so. He was not bound to wait for 90 cents or 80 cents or 50 cents; if he wanted to, he could go and sell his wheat for 60 cents to the wheat board. Then he could get his participation certificate and wait until the end of the crop year. He might get 20 cents or 10 cents or nothing. But he judged, not the government; he determined, not the government; he was taking the chance of winning something on the increased price of wheat if there was one, and he took the chance of getting nothing if there was nothing.
He could not lose.

He might, if wheat
dropped below 60 cents.
But he was to get 60 cents.

He could not get less than 60 cents, if that is what the hon. gentleman means. But he had a right to that alternate market, and that alternate market has been denied him. The essence of our whole effort in this house in July, 1935, was to provide the farmer of western Canada with an alternate market: private trade, public buyer- which? In the one case you take your money and say, "Good-bye, I am through"; in the other you take your money and your participation certificate, and you may get something or you may not.
Was it the intention of the government that the wheat board legislation should be of a permanent nature?

It was intended that if circumstances made it requisite, it was there. That is the reason why in committee I pointed out that a provision which would automatically lapse was unsound; that conditions in this world are so uncertain that we should have it there, and that if the time came

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
when it was thought desirable to repeal it we could do so. But parliament would do it, not we.
But as long as it was there, it would have to be operated.
Quite, until parliament repealed it.

But the intention in the first instance, I take it, was not that it was of a permanent nature. My right hon. friend said it would be there in case it were needed. So it necessarily follows that years might come when it would not be needed; then what becomes of the alternative market of which my right hon. friend speaks?

As long as the statute remained on the statute books, it was to be operated. We declined to consider the proposal made in the committee or in this chamber to make possible its automatic lapsing, believing that parliament itself must consider all the circumstances before the statute should cease to be part of the machinery of this country for dealing with the wheat crop.
I was merely trying to establish what was in the mind of the then government. Was this alternative market, of which my right hon. friend speaks so highly, always to be preserved for the farmer?

That was for parliament to consider. In the light of the conditions that then prevailed, we believed the statute should be continued until parliament decided otherwise; that is the fair way to put it.

At the first session of this parliament we in this corner moved a resolution urging the government to guarantee the farmers of western Canada a minimum price for wheat based on the cost of production. At this time we should like again to take the opportunity of urging on the government that they fix a price based on the cost of production of wheat. A little while ago the minister stated there would be a wheat board, there would be a fixed price and there would be participation. A little later he qualified that, saying that we might or might not have a wheat board in operation this fall; that is, the wheat board may be buying wheat or it may not. We may have a fixed price based on the cost of production, or again it may not be based on the cost of production. We may have participation, or on the other hand we may not have participation.

If the board buys wheat, you will have participation.
[Mr. Bennett.J

But you are not guaranteeing that you are going to buy wheat. In other words, the first statement really meant nothing. It means that there will be a fixed price, but there is no guarantee what the price will be, it may be only 20 cents a bushel. And there is no guarantee that the wheat board is going to operate. So we take this opportunity again to urge the government that the wheat board shall operate this fall, no matter what the price; that is, that the wheat board shall buy wheat irrespective of whether the market price falls below the fixed price; and, second, that the fixed price shall be definitely based on the cost of production.

I urge upon
the government that when setting the price of wheat they do not forget durum wheat, because Manitoba farmers, and I believe many farmers in Saskatchewan, are very much concerned about the price they are likely to get for durum wheat.
I do not like the way in which the government handled wheat during the last two years, but I am sure the western farmers will be very much pleased to have the announcement made by the minister to-day. I know it was made before, but I believe it was more specific to-day. We know now that we are going to have a board and a minimum price, and that there will be participation certificates. When the government are setting that price I urge that they be not afraid to make it fairly high. I believe the government are afraid that we shall get a 400 million bushel wheat crop this year. The best thing that could happen to Canada to-day would be to get a wheat crop of that size. It would solve the railway problem and the relief problem-there would be no need of relief-business would be good; the revenues of the country would be greatly increased, and Canada would have much less trouble in financing than she has to-day.
I am sure western Canada would make this offer to all Canada, that if the tariff be done away with she will ask for no relief and no protected price on wheat. Let industry stand on its own feet and the farmers of the country will stand on theirs. I know western Canada is willing and able to make that offer. I hope the government will not forget the durum wheat growers of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

The old man has
now got his second wind, and intends to use it. Pardon me if I take a minute or two to unlimber my ammunition wagon.

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
The things we have been speaking about this afternoon are as chicken-feed compared with what I should like to tell the committee if I can stick it out-and I am going to stick it out. I have my braces on; I left my belt off. But I have in its place, we hope, my shield and buckler.
Three years ago, more or less, I received from John Glossop, the superintendent of the old government terminal elevator at Port Arthur, a communication in which he made a large number of serious charges, and a number of helpful suggestions as well, with regard to the carrying on of that terminal elevator under the auspices of the McCabe Brothers, which had then been converted into a semi-public terminal. "Semi-public terminal" was always a misnomer; it is a mixing elevator, semi-mixing if you like, but altogether mixing now.
Glossop wrote me about February, 1935. There was no use in doing anything about those charges at that time, for the simple reason that you could not do anything with them successfully just before an election. It would always be cast up that it was an election dodge. Besides, I did not know then just what merit there was behind the charges, and not much about Mr. Glossop; although he had thirty years of experience in terminal elevators, and sixteen of those years were in the government owned terminal elevator. Therefore he was an employee of the government, and surely, holding that position for all those years, his statement should not be passed up carelessly. It came from him voluntarily; he had communicated first with Mr. Coote regarding the same matter. Mr. Coote could not see his way clear to take any action with the information, and before I had an opportunity to do so this grain commission was appointed. When they got into action I placed Mr. Glossop's charges in the hands of Mr. Ralston. counsel for the commission.
All I am going to tell hon. members now, or a great deal of it, has been placed before several members of the government, including the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance, and one other minister outside that grain sub-committee, whom I regarded very highly, and to whom I talked as man to man, as one privy councillor to another. I gave the same manuscript, the same statements regarding the administration of the grain act under the present chairman of the board of grain commissioners, to this minister, whose name I feel in honour bound not to mention, 'because I wanted to make sure that this information was getting to all the cabinet
and not merely those to whom I had sent this evidence. I hoped that between what I supplied them with and what they knew of me they would believe I was in earnest, and I hoped also they would take the initiative, without leaving it to me to investigate these matters and seeing to it that these practices were discontinued.
With regai-d to Mr. Ramsay, the chairman of the board, I gave the information to one of his colleagues when he was here about two weeks ago. I told Mr. Hamilton personally some of the things I am going to tell the committee now, so that the information would go to Mr. Ramsay and he would not be unprepared. I gave the same information to another hon. member who, I knew, would send it to the Minister of Mines and Resources. I gave everybody warning, so that I could not possibly be accused of taking advantage of my position here to make these statements in parliament. I did everything I could think of becoming a man so that everybody would be given fair warning.
Why should it be necessary for me to go into these matters? I have not time to go into them minutely, but I will go into them sufficiently to convince hon. members that it is time somebody took action in Canada if we are to preserve the quality of our wheat in the markets of the world. I know I am thought a hobbyist on this question, but I also know that the quality of our wheat is the one asset in the west that keeps us out of the poor-house. Tamper with the quality, and you strike at the very root of successful agriculture in the west. As I said a short time ago, ever since this act came into force, or at least ever since 1912, it has been violated at every opportunity; and if there were not an opportunity, one was made. Now it is my duty to show one more opportunity that has been and is being taken advantage of right up to this day.
I think I will tell my story without this confounded volume of evidence before me. It is so messed up, with four lawyers questioning Mr. Glossop, that it is hard to know just what he was saying. Like myself, he was pretty well bushed in the ears; he had a poor voice as well, and was not a very good witness. But out of the mouths of babes and sucklings-and even the Mr. Glossops- sometimes comes wisdom. I have here some eighteen charges that he made, giving the dates, the boats and the mixtures that went out of this McCabe elevator, where the mixing of the four top grades was prohibited. These questions came before this royal grain commission, with all these lawyers, and this is

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
what was said by the commissioner himself, if you please:-
The board of grain commissioners is the proper tribunal to hear these charges. Whatever evidence is taken here or whatever other evidence need not be taken here should be forwarded to the board.
That is, the board of grain commissioners, whose conduct was under observation, and who would be sitting in judgment on themselves. Is that not a remarkable thing? Then Mr. Ralston said:
I was not going into these in detail, but I was going to have him speak generally of his knowledge of these transactions-
He is referring to Mr. Glossop now.
-reported here and then turn him over to my learned friends for any examination they may have.
That is, to Mr. Pitblado, Mr. Coyne and Mr. Haffner, the last gentleman representing McCabe Brothers.. Then Mr. Glossop refers to the J. J. Donovan and two parcels of 10,000 bushels each.
That was one of the last parcels before you left?
A. Yes.
Q. What took place there?
A. An order for ten thousand bushels of No. 4 Northern was shipped in one hold. After the boat left the superintendent was told by the inspection department the grade was too low. Arrangements were made for the boat's return for an additional 10,000 bushels of 4 Northern. This second lot was made up of 3 Northern and Garnet tough 2 Northern, the average of the two lots making up the grade.
The particular offence charged here was allowing a boat, after it had received a grade, to come back and have that grade jacked up by the addition of other wheat. I think that was the outstanding offence here, because most people take it for granted, that No. 1 cannot be mixed with No. 4, though in my opinion this is very doubtful. I merely refer to this to show the committee, as I will in another place also, that Mr. Ramsay, the administration of whose department was in question, according to his own evidence knew there was some reflection being made on him. But what a glorious prospect it is for a potential offender to be given an opportunity of reviewing and sitting in judgment upon his own conduct! I know of only one other case of that kind in history. We might well go on a jaunt and a jag if the officer in charge would hand us over to ourselves for condemnation or approbation, to adjudicate upon ourselves.
There is one notable example, however, of this being tried once before. There is no record of it, because the records all disappeared somehow, but it was the famous or, if you like the other word, the infamous Hyndman commission. Those who did not like that

commission called it infamous; those who did like it omitted the prefix. That commission never reported. I searched the library in vain to find any vestige or trace of a report by the Hyndman commission. There is no doubt that it sat all through the west, right out to Alberta, through broad Saskatchewan and a little bit in Manitoba.
Then we find a man named Henderson occupying the same position in the United Grain Growers terminal elevator as Mr. Glossop occupied in the government elevator at Port Arthur for many years, until 1933, that of superintendent. The United Grain Growers were outraged at the thought that their business was being investigated. I have before me a resolution passed by the Canadian Council of Agriculture, and if necessary I can refer to another one drawn up by the vice-president of the United Grain Growers, whose name for the moment I have forgotten. In the document before me we find what they said about what they considered at that time to be an outrage.
But what was done last summer or last fall? In this instance, they handed over the charges to the one whose conduct was under observation and asked him to look into the matter-to look into his own conduct-and to report later to the commission. So that in the last instance we have the government passing the buck to the royal grain commission, and the commission passing the buck to Mr. Ramsay. Good Mr. Ramsay in due course passed the buck to Doctor Geddes, whose report will be recited in a few moments. This is what the resolution set out:
That to appoint as a member of the inquiry board-
And this was the Hyndman commission. Possibly I would do well to first give the names of the gentlemen who formed that commission. These were men of renown and of high standing in the community. Hon. members of the legal profession will know Mr. Justice Hyndman who, I understand, is now resident in Ottawa. Before I forget it may I say that a member of the library staff informed me he telephoned Mr. Justice Hyndman to ask where his report could be found, and said that it could not be found in the library. Mr. Justice Hyndman stated that he never did give a report. Well, now, that is funny- never did give a report. No evidence of Mr. Henderson which was taken before itl
Nothing daunted at my lack of success in tracing the history of this wonderful commission

and I do not say that in any offensive way-I found this information in the Canadian Annual Review of 1921. That is not

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
necessarily an official document, not at all; but it is usually fairly authentic. If any hon. member or minister thinks he is unjustly dealt with in this matter, he will have an opportunity to say where the record is wrong. It is the only record I can find. If the real record is not to be found, I cannot be blamed for taking the next best. I want to get at the facts, and to find the precedent for the present chairman of the board of grain commissioners being handed an opportunity of trying himself and of reporting back to the commission. This is what is contained in paragraph 2 at page 469 of the Canadian Annual Review:
That to appoint as a member of the inquiry board one who for nine years (Mr. Staples) has sat as a member of the board of grain commissioners, and whose failure properly to administer the grain act would constitute the principal ground for appointing a board of inquiry, is a fundamental breach of the principles of any inquiry conducted in the spirit of British law, and, therefore, is highly undesirable in the public interest.
If we apply that language, which was expressed with respect to the United Grain Growers and officers thereof, to the present situation, it would seem that this is exactly what was done by the royal grain commission of 1936-37 with the chairman of the board of grain commissioners. That is almost incredible, is it not? Here are the names of the commissioners: Hon. J. D. Hyndman, of the Alberta bench; W. D. Staples, of Fort William-the gentleman who was a member of the board of grain commissioners-J. H. Haslam, of Regina, and Lincoln Goldie, of Guelph. That was a pretty well qualified 'body of men; quite as good as the average, I would say.
If you will notice, in those days they were not satisfied with only one royal commissioner. There were four on that commission. Despite that fact, there is no record of any report given or of any evidence taken.
The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) was at that time president of the United Grain Growers. He may correct me if I am wrong, because I have only this book and the newspaper files in the library from which I can get information in the matter. When the evidence of Henderson was given in which an affidavit was provided by a gentleman whose name I do not recall, making statements with regard to false bottoms in sixteen or eighteen bins of the United Grain Growers, rather than let the matter proceed farther my hon. friend the Minister of Mines and Resources, together with thirty other elevator men, applied before Judge Galt of Winnipeg, or some other judge-that does not matter-for an injunction to restrain the 51952-283
Hyndman commission from going farther into the investigation of the United Grain Growers elevator. When any person puts himself in the position of stopping an inquiry rather than having the truth told, the information which might come out must have been rather terrible to contemplate. I could not come to any other conclusion. And that gentleman is one of the advisers of the present Prime Minister in connection with wheat matters. However, I shall let that stand for the moment.
It would appear that this kind of thing is infectious because it is being carried on now. Mark the stage of my story: The royal grain commissioners have passed the buck to Mr. Ramsay. Let us see what Mr. Ramsay has done with the buck. I shall not talk about the little frills in connection with what was done to the government terminal elevator at Port Arthur. But just by way of experiment and to clear the decks, reverting to mixing, may I point out that the letter from Mr. Glossop was the first information I received that the government elevator had been leased to a mixing elevator. That shocked me at the time. When you remember that there was no other public terminal left at Port Arthur at that time you can understand why I was shocked. This public terminal elevator was built by the Borden government at the request of the western farmers. What for? So that they might be sure that there was at least one elevator through which grain could be passed without fear of vulgar contamination. This elevator operated for many years and made a profit nearly all that time. Mr. Heatherington stated that the elevator had earned three times its cost up to that time. Under date of March 14, 1935, I asked the government the following questions:
1.	Is the federal government terminal elevator at Port Arthur still being operated by the government ?
2.	If not, (a) to whom was it leased; (b) when was it leased; (c) what were the terms and duration of such lease.
Here are the answers:
1.	No.
2.	(a) McCabe Brothers Grain Company Limited.
Just incidentally let me say that this company is recognized as one of the worst wheat mixers at the head of the lakes. There are degrees of mixing, and when it becomes too great it is no wonder that our wheat goes overseas in bad and irregular condition. There is probably such a thing as decent mixing, but this is a hog mixer who goes the limit -and teaches others to go the same pace. The



Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
fact is that the Department of Trade and Commerce leased a public terminal elevator at Port Arthur which had been asked for by the farmers of the west as part of their bill of rights. This is another illustration of how the Department of Trade and Commerce handles the grain of this country. Here are the rest of the questions:
3.	Did the government cease operating this public terminal elevator and lease it to a private concern?
4.	If so, for what reason?
The answer given to No. 3 is "answered by Nos. 1 and 2." You have to go back to Nos. 1 and 2 to get the answer, but I am not going to do that. The answer to No.4 is:
Owing to private interests in the grain trade acquiring greater storage capacity of their own, as also smaller crops and greater quantities of grain going out through Vancouver and Port Churchill, the government elevator at Port Arthur had been operating at a loss for the two preceding years, and the board of grain commissioners recommended that it should be leased.
When an institution has been earning good profits for fifteen or twenty years and then suffers a loss for a couple of years, is that justification for leasing to someone else? This elevator was asked for by the farmers of the west, but that is what happened. It was simply a case of clearing the decks to prepare for what was to follow. It was from this source that we obtained the first information that the elevator had been leased. Nothing that we have seen had been said about it in the newspapers or anywhere else. Section 125 contained the mandatory prohibition against mixing. Every effort was made to show that there were some reservations in connection with that. Let me quote from the evidence given before the commission. The royal commission was dealing with smutty and other rejected grains, and Mr. Ramsay is examined by Mr. Coyne as follows :
Q. That was the act of 1925?
A. That was the act of 1925. When this act was redrafted and revised in 1929, through some reason, possibly through an oversight, section 103 was omitted.
Those who have anything to do with the legal or departmental revision of statutes understand how sections can be dropped inadvertently, but when that happens too frequently you prick up your ears to find out what is happening. The result of this omission was that, from 1930 on, the Canada Grain Act contained no statutory basis for these off grades. It left them out on a limb, as it were. Hon. members can look up the old section 103 if they want to. I wish these

documents would rise up themselves to give witness against these things. My eyesight is not so good, and I have no doubt the document I want is right on top here but I cannot see it. Of course, one does not see as well under these trying conditions. Here is what happened. Testimony was given before the Brown commission in Saskatchewan and accepted by the federal government. Mr. Ramsay had that to go to, recommending no mixing of dry and tough wheat, as a guide when he found that section 103 had been lost. Lost? It was not lost.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to show what the chairman of the board of grain commissioners was doing by way of sitting up and making the best defence he could. I referred to the losing of section 103 as one of his experiences. I think maybe he was disappointed. The section was this; I read it to show its importance:
103. All good grain that has an excessive moisture, being tough, damp or wet or otherwise unfit for warehousing, shall be entered on the inspecting officer's books as "No grade," with his notations as to quality and condition.
2.	All grain that is in a heating condition or is badly bin-burnt, whatsoever grade it might otherwise be, shall be reported and entered upon the inspecting officer's books as "Condemned," with the inspector's notations as to quality and condition.
3.	All grain that is unsound, musty, dirty, smutty or sprouted, or that contains a large admixture of other kinds of grain, seeds or wild oats, or from any other cause is unfit to be classed under any of the recognized grades, shall be classed as "Rejected," with the inspector's notations as to quality and condition.
4.	All grain shall be weighed and the weight per bushel recorded in the inspecting officer's book.
5.	No grain that has been subject to scouring or treatment by use- of lime or sulphur shall be graded higher than No. 3.
This last is supposed to refer to what was, in the old days, smutty grain.
It can easily be said by pro-mixers that the omission of that section has no significance; that it neither legalizes nor prohibits. Anticipating that objection, might I refer to another lost "Charley Ross"-you know who Charley

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
Ross, of long ago is,-lost in the statutes of 1929. That emanated as a result of a terrible struggle in camera in the subcommittee, which about put me "on the hummer" before we got through. I remember that we wrestled over this particular section, knowing the predisposition of the trade and commerce department, largely through ignorance, or rather, through want of information, throughout the years, right from the days of Sir Richard Cartwright down to the present day. I know them all-giant intellects except as regards wheat. Here is the section we wrestled over; that is the reason I missed it. It is section 140 subsection 1A of the Canada Grain Act of 1929:
Private elevators when so licensed may carry on the business of mixing grain and grades of grain except grain of the grades mentioned and defined in section ninety-six of the act under the heading "Spring Wheat" and more particularly described therein as No. 1 Manitoba Hard, No. 1 Manitoba Northern, No. 2 Manitoba Northern and No. 3 Manitoba Northern."
These are definitely described grades in which mixing must not be done. Here is another clause, subsection 2 of section 18 of the old act and section 84 of this; it is a very important one to be lost:
No grain while being received into, while in store in, or while being shipped out of any public elevator, shall be mixed one grade with another or with anything else whatsoever.
There is nothing left out there; in order to make assurance doubly sure, that was put in, but it was inadvertently dropped from the consolidating act of 1930. If anybody can find it there, I shall be the first to thank him, because if it is in the 1930 act my case is stronger than ever.
I was endeavouring to show how my friend the chairman of the board was getting along examining himself. At page 12,244 of the evidence taken before the royal commission I read this:
Q. The reason for rejection would be given so that you would have a number of off grades, all attached as satellites to 1 Northern, and similarly for all the other straight grades?
This was asked by Mr. Coyne of Mr. Ramsay. He answered "yes".
Q. That was the act of 1925?
A. That was the act of 1925.
The witness Mr. Ramsay goes on:
When this act was redrafted and revised in 1929, through some reason, possibly through an oversight, section 103 was omitted.
I referred to that before.
Consequently the Canada Grain Act from 1930 provides no statutory basis for these off grades.
It is too long to quote it all. Later on the statement is made:
The omission is serious. . .
I should think it was. It makes all the difference between mixing and not mixing.
. . . particularly with respect to tough grain where the quantity is often quite important. Primary inspections for the western division from 1925-36 report 6,721 ears of tough grain. The other "off" grades included 642 cars of damp grain, 703 cars of smutty grain and 349 cars of rejected grain, rejected for being sprouted, heated, mixed with gravel.
Mr. Chairman, do you know where those are going now? A great many of them, if not all, are going into the straight grades, after that little section I read, which has been lost, which stated that nothing else, nothing which you can conceive of, shall be or can be put into the straight grades.
The failure to provide for the off grades was discovered when the act was put into effect in the autumn of 1930. Confronted with this difficulty, the board instructed the chief inspector to prepare classifications covering grain of this nature. At the meeting of the grain standards committee of that year, the subject was discussed, and the classifications prepared were approved as proper specifications to cover out of condition grain and mixtures.
This is what he is saying. He authorized this himself, without any statute to back it up. This is about as bad as the government itself was with respect to the order in council, the rider to which I referred that rode out the wheat board in 1936. Like priest, like people; like master, like men; this is an infectious sort of riding, apparently.
The other phase of the problem was how were cars marked as off grade grain to be handled when they reached the terminals.
He knew there was a question there, or he would not have said that. What should be done with it when it reached1 the terminals? Let us see.
The board decided in accordance with previous practice-
Yes, in accordance with practice in the old mixing days when it was as wide open as a barn door.
-to provide for the treatment of the grain where practical, with a view to placing it after treatment in the grade to which it would belong originally had it been in satisfactory condition.
There you are, manoeuvring first to get rid of the big government terminal at Port Arthur through which the grain could go without any mixing, and after clearing the decks for that, they come along with this ingenious device of mixing wheat for the purpose of drying it-mixing dry wheat with tough wheat, making the dry wheat absorb the surplus water in the tough wheat, thereby enabling them to get the mixture into the

Supply-Trade-Grain Commission
straight grades and sell at the same time thousands of tons of good water, in the form of either spray or water from the clouds. At any rate, it was water, and the more water you have in grain the lower the price you get for it, because one of the price determining factors in grain is its moisture content. That is something which has never been gone into properly. When I was on the other side in 1928 I met a man with many others sitting around the board room of the Liverpool corn exchange who assured me they were positive that Canadian wheat was sprayed somewhere in transit, perhaps at the head of the lakes. If these practices are abroad as above alleged, they should be run down and discovered and disclosed, and not covered up.
Carried.

I do not know what that remark was, but I do not care; it may have been good, or it may have been bad. I hope I am not hurting anyone, and I am awfully sorry that I cannot hear. The minister might come a little closer and we would both be better off; but ministers do not do that these days, though they used to. When we had a majority of only one we would move along the front line anywhere you wanted, but when there is a majority of 101 they are not so particular. But that is always the way. This is the best defence, remember, that could be put up by the chairman of the board of grain commissioners. If he has any other, he has not disclosed it. I continue:
Q. Section 125, subsection (1), reads:
""All western grain received into any licensed public terminal elevator shall be binned with grain of the same grade, and not otherwise."
A. This is merely pointing out that the act does carry exceptions to the mandatory section 125 in regard to the handling of the first four grades.
What do you know about that? 'That is Mr. Ramsay's answer, remember. In my opinion the section which he contends did that was inserted afterwards, just as the other ones were previously lost. That is the result of my investigation, and again I shall be glad to apologize if it does not prove to be the case, because I want someone in authority to get to the bottom of this thing and see that I am not flimflamming. The truth is too bad already without making it worse by exaggeration.
Q. This section 138 (6) may only say that you can bin this commercial grain which has been altered with one of the other statutory grades, and not the first four?
A. Mr. Coyne: Yes. It is really a question-
This is Mr. Coyne. Some nasty person has suggested that he has a woolsack appoint-
IMr. Motherwell.]
ment around the corner, but that is what mean people say:-
It is really a question whether section 125 governs section 138 (6) or whether section 138 (6) is an absolute exception.
The Commissioner:	Yes, whether section

May I say a word by way of digression? A very good friend of mine said before we started this evening: Why didn't you bring this on earlier in the session? Will anyone tell me one moment when I could have brought it on before?
I have not the bringing of it on. Was I not rapping at the door of many ministers urging them to look into this? I do not want to be taunted now with killing time when we all want to go home. We all do; so do I. But I had not the bringing of it on. I went as far in the debate on the address as it was decent to do. The commission had not yet reported. I strained a point in giving the government a hint. Hon. members will remember that I said I wanted a self-supporting board, and also a non-hibernating one, and the commission had not reported. That was going as far as I dared go, recognizing the proprieties at all, before the commission reported. Then Mr. Coyne and Mr. Ramsay go on. Mr. Ramsay said:
We have never had a suitable opportunity to amend the act until last year.
I wonder what that means.
That was before we knew you, Mr. Commissioner, would look into this matter. The question is now in the hands of the government.
Let us analyse that. It is strange how we can read a thing and see nothing in it. I gave some of my old colleagues a hint of what was in it, but I do not think they saw it. There is such a thing as seeing and not perceiving, hearing and not understanding. I know something about the latter. Let us see what he says:
We have never had a suitable opportunity to amend the act until last year.
That was said in 1937. Parliament had met at ieast seven times, since 1929, in three of which sessions the grain act was before this house. Why did they not take one of those three times, or one of the seven times? Probably the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) will answer that after consulting his coachers. I will answer it for him in one possible way other than what I
have mentioned. I have told this to some friends too. Possibly Mr. Ramsay tried to get amendments made, tried to have these deficiencies corrected, these lost Charley Rosses found, but his minister would not listen. Maybe I should not say that, but I am between the devil and the deep sea. I want to be fair to Mr. Ramsay; I almost want to make an excuse for him. If he went to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who was over him during that period from 1929 until now and recommended that the necessary remedial legislation be introduced and was refused-well let them have it out between them.

I protest against the actions of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in connection with this grant of $600,000 that we have -been giving them every year for the service between Canada, China and Japan. In 1936 I introduced a resolution asking that they be called upon, before they received any more subsidy, to -have their ships manned mostly by Canadians. This matter was referred to a committee of the house; the committee met; evidence was called from the Pacific coast, the Canadian Pacific Steamships were represented, likewise the seamen. That committee brought in a report recommending that the company be called upon as a start to take the Chinamen off the decks of their ships and replace them by Canadian seamen. I am going to take a moment to read the recommendation of the committee of 1936:
That, as up to the year 1913 the decks of the Empress boats were manned by white seamen, and inasmuch as the deck service is an important and responsible branch of the work of these boats, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company be requested to replace the orientals now so employed by Canadian seamen, and that this change be made at the company's earliest opportunity.
This report was presented to the house and adopted unanimously. No action however was taken by Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited, so in -1937 I again introduced this resolution. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) was in Australia, and his duties were being carried on for the time being by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). On suggestion of the latter minister 1 withdrew the resolution at that time rather than press it to a vote, because he stated that he would set up a committee on the Pacific coast to find out if the contention of the company was correct, that there were not enough white, Canadian seamen there to work the decks of the ships. So Mr. Kerr, inspector of subsidized steamship services, was sent there and, with Mr. F. E. Harrison, representing the Department of Labour, and Mr. J. A. McGowan, shipping master of Vancouver, formed the committee which held an inquiry, and I am going to take a moment or two to give their findings. 
At this late stage of the session I have not time to go into the matter as fully as I should like, -but briefly they advertised and asked for experienced seamen who would be available for employment on these steamships. In response some 380 experienced seamen were registered, and here is the recommendation of the committee:
In addition to the above mentioned seamen, a very large number of young men presented themselves and expressed a desire to sail in Canadian Pacific trans-Pacifie vessels if employment on deck could be found. The navy league, sea cadet corps, has about 200 youths between the ages of 12 and 18 in training at Vancouver and Victoria.
These would be available, and they are very anxious to obtain this employment. Here is the final part of the recommendation of the committee that went out to the Pacific coast and investigated the entire situation:-
The committee is of opinion that the deck departments of two Canadian Pacific ships could be manned by the seamen shown in the third classification above mentioned, which contains men with statable experience in oceangoing vessels, and that the change-over in the remaining ships should be possible within a reasonable time by transferring a number of experienced men to those vessels and drawing on selected types in other classifications.
For the benefit of the committee I repeat that on these four ships there are some 1,783 Chinese from Hongkong, who are not British subjects, but who are Chinese in the strict interpretation of the word. The first recommendation requested that the deckhands of these ships be replaced and that white men be given preference, and this latter committee of 1937 found that 380 fully experienced seamen were available, and should replace the Chinamen. So I maintain that the Canadian Pacific should be compelled to comply with the recommendation adopted by this house in 1936. which recommendation was not carried out either last year or this year. I say by their attitude they have actually defied this House of Commons, by their contempt for a recommendation so made by this house.
There are seventy Chinese on each deck. It is well known that one white man can replace two or even three Chinese, so on each of these ships thirty-five white men could take over the work and comply with all the regulations of the shipping act, if given a chance. I am taking great exception to that fact that they have not been given this chance. I am taking exception to this subsidy being actually granted, and I am sorry that it has not been possible to air this matter in the house before this late hour. I had a resolution in this connection on the order paper this session, but only one resolution can be brought for-

Supply-Trade-Subsidies
ward at a time, and so mine was not reached.
I am going to appeal to the minister, and if the Canadian Pacific is not brought to time I am serving notice now that if I am here next year they will have quite a good deal more trouble in getting this subsidy through. I think it is a travesty of justice for the Canadian Pacific to set itself above the house and defy what I claim to be an order of parliament. In Vancouver we have men by the hundreds walking the streets who would gladly take positions on these ships if given a chance, and in view of all the inquiry that has been made I should like to hear what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to say as to why this recommendation has not been carried out.

I should like to assure the hon. member for New Westminster that the department is not unmindful of the report of the committee with regard to the replacement of the Chinese on this service with white men. The matter has been very fully discussed; I have repeatedly brought it to the attention of the Canadian Pacific. I am not sure that I should go into all the details at the moment, but the arguments that were advanced, it seemed to me, made it inopportune to press too strongly for the withholding of the subsidy. Perhaps for the time being at least it might satisfy the committee and my hon. friend if I read a letter from the chairman of Canadian Pacific Steamships, Limited, in which he offers to make at least some concession at the moment. I am not making any commitment as to what might be done later. Sir Edward Beatty writes me as follows :
For a number of years each of our ships has been carrying from eight to ten youths for training as pursers, stewards, etc. These youths serve first of all in the deck department as bridge messengers, and, as such, they learn discipline, ship's routine, and the interdependent relation of the various branches of the ship's staff.	.	,
We propose to add an additional six to each ship (or twenty-four in all) in the deck department, to be classed as ordinary seamen as soon as qualified, and to receive regular instruction in seamanship, so as to qualify for the rating of A.B., when they have accumulated the necessary legal time at sea.
As soon as we have six qualified A.B.s, we would replace the Chinese quartermasters with these white boys, who should eventually be able to obtain a certificate as second mate, and, in due time, as mate and master.
These boys would be drawn through the navy league, where they would have obtained useful preliminary training, and are good material for the R.C.N.V.R.
Our plan has the entire approval of the naval branch of the Department of National Defence, who more than once have expressed a willingness, if the necessary funds were forthcoming, to assist in the training of these young men.
There should be no undue delay in giving effect to this plan, as soon as the necessary
living and sleeping quarters can be provided, and it can be in operation in a very short time.
Yours very truly,
E. W. Beatty,
Chairman.
What is the date of that letter?

There is just one difficulty that has been overlooked by the hon. member for New Westminster when he suggests that this is defiance of parliament. A subsidy is an act of parliament; both houses agree, and the crown assents. A resolution of a committee of the House of Commons would not be sufficient to withhold a subsidy; and until such time as it is approved and becomes an act of parliament .by being passed by the senate and approved by the crown, it would not rank with the appropriation bill so that we would be able to give effect to it. Surely the hon. member has overlooked that fact.
I have had occasion to look into the matter.

I appreciate the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition and realize that what he says is perhaps true. But here we have a committee of the house going into all the facts in 1936, hearing the Canadian Pacific on the one hand and the seamen on the other, and bringing in a report recommending that the Canadian Pacific take steps to man the decks at least, with white, Canadian seamen. They do not do so. In 1937 another committee is set up, and it finds that 380 experienced seamen are available; yet the Canadian Pacific say there are not sufficient men with which to man these steamships. I say that if this country means anything at all to Sir Edward Beatty, he should at least give a lead to Canadians, especially in these times of stress, when thousands of our citizens are walking the streets. There are hundreds of men in Vancouver who are willing and ready to go on these ships if they were given a chance.

The Canadian Pacific just says there are not enough men available. I say that is not true, and a position which should not be tolerated. If it were not for the lateness
