I have a few observations to make regarding statements made bv the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) when the item was under discussion on a previous occasion. I believe he left the impression that in connection with the operation of traps the Fraser River Fishermen's Protective Association were in favour of the retention of traps. I want absolutely to refute that statement.
Immediately the statement was made in the house a telegram was received by me from the association protesting strenuously against the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo. On that occasion the hon. member quoted from a book entitled Net Profits, published this year under the auspices of the Fraser River Fishermen's Protective Association. He quoted one paragraph. Although it makes no definite statement, it does say this:
Based upon the experiences of past years, when groups employing different modes of fishing have vied for position to strengthen their particular interests in this fishery, the necessity of maintaining status quo in the industry becomes apparent.
The hon. member for Nanaimo left the impression on the house and perhaps the country also that by that statement appearing in the booklet Net Profits, the fishermen's protective association of the city of New Westminster were in favour of the retention of traps.
On the day following I received a telegram in which they emphatically denied that statement, saying it was not true. They are hoping traps will be eliminated before long, and I want the house and the country to know they are opposed and will continue their opposition until the traps are removed.
I shall take another minute to refute a further statement in regard to the number of men employed. Possibly I should say I make these observations for purposes of refuting the hon. member's statement, and I do so to draw the facts to his attention and to the attention of the minister. Last year these traps caught a total of 311,438 fish. There were forty men employed, making an average catch of 6,228 fish per man, whereas in the whole Fraser area in Puget Sound the average catch was 745 fish per man.
These figures are striking. Those who want the fish traps taken out of there are anxious
to employ more labour, realizing that the traps not only deprive men of their livelihood, but also to a certain extent ruin the fish. The two companies in question have an investment of $100,000, but I must point out that that is not their own money. Of that they have only a total investment of $12,000 each. One year they made a profit of $24,800, which shows this is another case of vested interests being protected. I would suggest to the minister that instead of charging a licence fee of $500 a year, he might very well raise the amount. I venture to predict there are men in British Columbia who would be willing to pay $5,000 to be allowed to operate those traps. I am sorry I have not the time to go into the matter fully, but I wish to reassure the committee and the hon. member for Nanaimo that the fishermen of the Fraser river are absolutely opposed to traps, and want them entirely eliminated.
I have just one observation to make. I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he is a member of the international sockeye commission.
Yes.
Does he carry into the meetings of that commission his prejudice against the Sooke traps?
I do not think I should answer a question like that by the hon. gentleman. It is not that I am afraid to answer it, but he has no right to ask me that question.
If the hon. gentleman is taking his prejudices into the meetings of that commission, he has no right to be a member.
I dispute that statement. I have every right to be on the commission, and represent the gill net fishermen on that commission.

Since this matter was last before the committee, two things have happened which, I think, have a bearing on the situation. The first is a resolution passed by the Kyuquot Trailers Cooperative Association, one of the oldest and largest and most successful fishermen's cooperative associations in British Columbia. This is dated June 25, 1938, and reads:
The members of the Kyuquot Trailers Cooperative Association, Victoria, B.C., at their semi-annual meeting held at Kyuquot, deplore and protest against the continued issuance of trap licences in British Columbia, considering it an unfair privilege, that excludes other fishing gear from operation within such fixed location, and also as a destructive measure which does not distinguish between legal size nor out of season fish.
Supply-Fisheries

They pass this resolution every time they meet. It will be recalled that when this matter was last before the committee the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) read a brief which had been prepared for him by one of the trap owners. At that time he stated that the resolution against traps had been railroaded through the meeting of the associated boards of trade of Vancouver island by myself at the meeting held a year ago. Under date of February 1, the hon. member wrote to the minister to call attention to the fact that this resolution was of small value; that it was wrongly presented and hastily passed. He stated that it met with strenuous opposition from the Victoria board of trade, a far superior board. Something has happened since then which throws some light on the matter. The associated boards of trade of Vancouver island have held another meeting. That is a very representative body, a parliament in itself. The members act without pay, and they have a fine idea of their duties and responsibilities as citizens. They met at Courtenay the other day, and this subject was brought up and discussed for three hours. The resolution was not railroaded through by me because I was not there. Mr. Todd, one of the moneyed principals in this matter was there, as well as Mr. Goodrich, another member. I understand there was also a lawyer along. After a debate of three hours a vote was taken, and only seven votes out of a total of thirty were in favour of traps. Everything possible was done to secure a verdict favourable to traps; but after a full discussion, that little parliament of Vancouver island, representing the best elements of the district, took an even stronger stand against traps than they had taken previously. It is true the Victoria board of trade was largely against this, but that board represents the moneyed interests. I am glad Vancouver island has shown its good sense by acting in this way.

I share the views expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), in regretting that the minister has seen fit to protect the privileged interests at Sooke and to disregard the welfare of the workers in a most important industry.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct attention. I have in my hand an urgent communication which was received this day from the fishermen in Parry Pass, Queen Charlotte islands, British Columbia, under date of June 21, 1938. I believe the

best way to place this matter before the committee will be to read the important paragraphs of this communication. They are:
On the Langara island trolling grounds approximately 400 fishermen (white and Indian) manage to eke out a living for themselves and their families, possibly 2,000 persons, by catching the spring salmon which are attracted there by a comparatively small colony of herring schooling in that vicinity.
Should, for some reason, these herring on which the salmon feed, disappear, it is obvious that the salmon would also disappear in search of other feeding grounds, thus closing the source of livelihood of the 400 fishermen and their dependents.
Until recently the possibility of this happening has seemed remote, but now through a lack of foresight on the part of our fishery department, it has become a real danger.
Having received a permit from the department, a herring seine boat is now removing this salmon feed by hauls of from 50 to 100 tons at a time (approximately half a million herring to a haul). At this rate the small school will not last long. They are decreasing a.nd as they go the salmon catch is also decreasing.
Appeals to the department seem to be in vain. Not an unusual thing when the person appealed against is the wealthy operator. The replies received from the department are not convincing to practical fishermen. For instance mention of no control outside the three mile limit when the herring are being caught within quarter of a mile of the shore, show that they are not even caring to investigate the matter, but are content to give an opinion from an armchair in the same office to which we send their salary cheques.
If these herring were being used for food purposes perhaps there would be less reason for grumbling but they are being reduced to fertilizer.
What inhuman system is this that allows a wealthy company to send out a single boat to take away for all time the means of livelihood of 2,000 people? And all for the sake of the profits on a few measly tons of fertilizer.
The resolution endorsed by the fishermen's committee and the councillors of the Indian tribe in the area reads as follows:
Whereas herring is being rapidly depleted on the northern coast of Graham island, Langara island in particular, and incidentally salmon being caught in the seine also, and
Whereas where herring have been depleted on their feeding grounds, such as the above mentioned, the grounds are also destroyed for salmon, and
Whereas we consider the use of this superior quality of herring in a reduction plant should be prohibited and conserved as much as possible for food purposes only, and
Whereas about 400 fishermen, Indians and whites (with their families about 2,000 persons), are dependent on those salmon grounds for their livelihood, and further, consider this $300,000 industry is of more importance to Canada than the operation of any reduction plant,
Therefore be it resolved that (at this joint meeting of Indians and white fishermen) we desire to take all legal means to protect our

Supply-Fisheries
source of living, but, we demand and intend that seining for herring on the above mentioned grounds be stopped.
I should like some assurance from the minister that this matter will be investigated and the interest of these fishermen properly
protected.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext: I have received a communication along lines similar to that just read. Last evening and this morning .we inquired from our officers on the Pacific coast, and we have been informed- that what happened there was that a boat has been prospecting during the last few days. We were told that there has been no fishing going on and that there is no likelihood of any fishing being carried on in those waters.

A moment ago when I was speaking I could not place my -hand on the telegram which I had received from the fishermen asking that immediate action be taken in connection with the Sooke traps. This telegram reads:
Any intimation that Fraser river fishermen wish Sooke traps to remain absolutely false. Every fishermen's organization on Pacific coast to the best of my knowledge want Sooke traps out immediately and expect action to this end from parliament this session.
Before I resume my seat may I say to the hon. member for Nanaimo that I was made a member of the international sockeye commission to represent the Fraser river fishermen. My views with regard to traps were well known before I was placed on that commission. I would be derelict in my duty if I did not support the Fraser river fishermen in their attitude against these traps and in their request for immediate action. In case I am misrepresented, I want to assure my hon. friend that I am opposed to the continuation of traps at Sooke.

Will the minister give us some assurance that if it is shown that seining for herring in the vicinity of Langara islands threatens the interests of the fishermen in that vicinity, it will be prohibited?
Certainly.

I do not think it is necessary for me to protest, but I hope the minister will study this question of the Sooke traps as he has done hitherto. I hope he will do this in the interests of the conservation of the salmon and in the light of the peculiar conditions under which these traps were established.
And the profits of the man who has the concession.

As regards the herring situation, I brought this up when this matter was before the house on April 26. It is a lifelong grievance on the Pacific coast, the reducing of herrings which are not very profitable to reduce because they are very small in oil content as compared with pilchards, and the fishermen claim, I think without contradiction, that they are the food of salmon. It is a well known saying among fishermen, "No herring, no salmon." That is, if the herring are scarce this year, the salmon run will be short.
The minister says they are only experimenting out there. Quite so, but what for? With a view of taking larger quantities for reduction. That is the sole purpose for which they are seining in the waters to which the hon. member for Vancouver North has alluded, and the reason why there has been no depletion there is because it had not been fished before. I would ask the minister if he will not yield this much to our representations: Why not put that area up there under the same conditions as obtain on the west coast of Vancouver island, where experience has shown it is absolutely essential to have a close season, and we have a close season running from February 5 to, I believe, October 1. That would give the herring at least half a chance.

As my hon. friend knows, under the present regulations there is restriction upon the quantity of herring to be caught in some areas. I understand it has been and I can assure him it is the policy of the department at the present time that when the catching of herring for reduction purposes is a menace to the salmon industry, the prohibition of fishing for herring is made and will be enforced.

Yes, but the only trouble is that it is not. There is a quota put on, yes. The quota is only that amount which the reducing plants want. I have in my possession a letter from the local minister saying that he was not going to allow herrings to be reduced on the west coast. A year later he announced that he had gone into the matter very thoroughly, and the dead limit he was going to allow was 20,000 tons.
That was the provincial minister.

Yes. But we have the control of the fishing. He said it would not go beyond
20,000	tons. I replied, saying, " Oh, yes, it will. The amount of the quota will be limited only by the desires of the reduction plants." Sure enough, next year, instead of
Supply-Fisheries

20,000	tons it was 40,000 tons. Before that season was over-even in that one season- it was raised again another 5,000 tons, raised up to 45,000 tons in the comparatively limited waters of Barkley sound and the west coast. My experience is that while a quota is put on and they say they will not allow it to be exceeded, that quota will be raised to whatever quantity the reduction plants want. The minister has had scientific men out there who have demonstrated, to their satisfaction at any rate, that herrings on the Pacific coast are being depleted. They proved that by the size of them. Long experience tells them that the depletion of a run is first indicated by those taken being smaller. That was demonstrated, and an expert sent in a report to that effect. My information is-I cannot prove it at the moment, but I think I could if I were given time-that the official got a hint not to send in reports like that because they were not acceptable at Ottawa.

All I can say is again to reassure my hon. friend that whenever it is demonstrated that fishing for herring in any waters is detrimental or a menace to the salmon industry, fishing for herring will be restricted.

With reference to the matter of herring being used for fertilizer, this is a subject which concerns not only the west coast but also the east coast. I have received letters from fishing organizations in tihe maritime provinces stating that a splendid market for herring could be obtained if there were instructions issued, by men properly trained to instruct fishermen, how to prepare the herring for market. Has the minister received any requests that a practical instructor, conversant with both French and English, be appointed by the department to instruct the fishermen of the Northumberland strait or any other part of the maritime provinces in the preparation of these herring for the market?

I do not recall having received any request from fishermen or residents along the Northumberland strait. My recollection is that in Charlotte county, the bay of Fundy and that district there is a very valuable herring industry, and we have instructors giving demonstrations and instructing the fishermen how to prepare their fish for the market. I believe the best herring that are processed and put into foreign markets and into our own markets come from that area and command the best prices.

The minister, then, is not
aware of any request from Westmorland or

Kent county in New Brunswick, or that section, for a bilingual instructor to instruct the fishermen in the preparation of herrings?
It is possible that a request has been made to the department, but at the moment I do not recollect any.

Item agreed to.
Building fishways and clearing rivers, $9,000.

The last time this item was up on a general basis I discussed the question of the fish ladder on the Puntledge river at Courtenay. The minister, no doubt, has had time to look into the matter. Has he any statement to make in connection with it?

The hon. member is correct. On the last occasion when the matter came before this committee I think I gave the information which was then before me, that is, that a fish ladder or fishway had been built in that river in 1922, had been washed out in 1927, was renewed in the same year, in 1935 was washed out again, and has been replaced.
And again last December.

And again last December was washed away. Since then there has been some difference of opinion as to whether the same kind of fishway should be built or a different method used. To build another fishway to meet the wishes of some people who are advocating a change, it is claimed, would impair the use of that river for water power development; and, looking over the files of the department, I find that there is a great difference of opinion between the residents of the locality, the company which is operating the water power-I think it is the Dunsmuir Collieries-and the engineers. Since then the local engineer of the department has reported that it would be costly and would not be as efficient as it is claimed to build a new type of fishway, and it would impair the use of that water power. However, I know that the citizens of the localities-I think these are Courtenay and Cumberland-have different views; and in order to settle the matter or set at rest the minds of these people, if it is agreeable that an independent engineer should pass upon the position, I am satisfied that this shall be done. My colleague the Minister of Public Works will lend me the use of his resident engineer or one of the staff on the Pacific coast to look over the situation and make a report as to what he thinks should meet the requirements.

I think that is a satisfactory suggestion, and I know the public works en-

Supply-Fisheries
gineer is a man of great ability. I have no doubt, therefore, his report will be exactly what he sees.
I want to say a word or two in connection with the statements that have been made to the effect that it would not be possible, or that at any rate it would be very difficult, to put the ladder up where it ought to be, namely, at the end of the dam. After being washed away three times, it is no use where it is; we must put it somewhere else, and the obvious place in which to put it is around the end of the dam in the rock. The departmental officials say that this would be dangerous to the dam on account of blasting. But you can blast anything, anywhere, if you are careful. I have blasted within three feet of the glass windows of my house without shattering the windows, and in the city you will see workmen using dynamite a few feet away from the sidewalk without any damage ensuing, because they know how to do it. They use discretion; they cover it up, and so on.
The next question is, Would it be workable? Well, we have an example of a fish ladder at Stamp falls in the neighbourhood of Alberni, and people come from far and near to see the fish going up the ladder pretty much as people go upstairs. That cost only
84,000	and the height was twenty-two feet. At Maggie lake the ladder was nineteen or twenty feet and it cost only $3,000. At the Puntledge riger the dam is fourteen feet at the outside, probably less. It would not, therefore, be a big undertaking and would not need more than six steps for the fish to jump from one pool to the other.
Let me give an illustration of what science can do. I allude to Bonnieville falls in the Columbia river where the fish have to ascend an average of fifty feet, lower at high water and higher at low water. The ladder is cut out of the rock on both sides. Of course, the higher the elevation the greater the cost. At Puntledge river they ascend fourteen feet at the most and less than that when the water is higher. The cost would not be deadly at all, and it would be a means of establishing a run there which used to be a valuable cohoe run and one that could be made into a sockeye run as well. I would remind the minister that the department pledged themselves, when they obtained the consent of the house, to do away with the policy of having hatcheries for the propagation of fish, to devote more money to the development of fish along natural lines, clearing out the rivers and putting in fish ladders. They put one in at Maggie lake last year in pursuance of that policy, and as we are saving large sums in connection with the
hatcheries, I suggest that we can well afford to undertake such work as I have indicated. The minister has made a statement about bringing in an outside engineer, and I am glad to see an independent man brought in, because a mistake was made about ten or fifteen years ago. We all make mistakes; but a mistake was made at that time, when the wrong type of ladder was put in, and it is difficult to get a local engineer to turn around and admit that he made a mistake. It is against human nature. I would be prepared, however, to accept the judgment of an independent engineer.

Item agreed to.
Development of the deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $62,000.

When this matter was up
before, I brought up the question of the prospect of a foreign power-it does not matter who they are-fishing off the shores of British Columbia in such a way as entirely to eliminate our industry. We are talking about fish traps and guardians, and all that sort of thing. But if the policy that I mention, which is being pursued by the foreign power in question, is continued, then the fisheries department, so far as British Columbia is concerned, might as well shut up shop, because there will not be any fish at all. That applies not only to cod and herring, but to halibut as well. We have built up a wonderful business in halibut under the United States treaty and that will be wiped out if the present policy is continued. The minister did not give me much encouragement before. He said I ought to have more confidence in the government and should know that matters of such importance would be considered in the way they ought to be. I am sorry, but I should like to get a little more information.
The situation is this. Three years ago there appeared off the shore of Alaska-it is Alaska to-day, but our funeral to-morrow-a large number of fishing boats belonging to the Japanese. The procedure was to bring a great mother ship from Japan and it would be loaded up with what, in the east, would be dories. They are small gas-driven motorboats, and they string a line of nets 200 miles long-I wish to impress that fact upon the committee 

right across the run of the fish making into Alaskan waters. Through the use of aeroplanes it is now possible to spot the fish far at sea and see the direction in which they are running, because fish do not run all over the ocean, but move in one concrete body towards a definite destination. It is therefore possible for the Japanese to run this line for 200
Supply

Fisheries

miles, as they have done more recently on the Russian shore and at a distance of ten or twenty or thirty miles out, entirely cut off the fish and there catch every fish that comes along. They are bothered with no restrictions. The Japanese idea of fishing in their own waters-and they demonstrated it there fairly well

is to take every fish they can possibly get. The Jap does not know the meaning of conservation, nor does he know anything about restricted hours or seasons. His idea is to take whatever is there, and when that is gone, to go somewhere else. They exhausted their own fisheries and then turned to the Russian fisheries. They are now beginning the same thing in Alaskan waters, and it is only a matter of a year or two when we shall find them taking the halibut banks off the British Columbia coast and the salmon runs going into the Fraser river and into all these rivers to which we have referred.
This is no idle dream of mine, because it is actually going on. I have a number of newspaper cuttings here, but I shall not read them. One or two of the headings are interesting. Here is one for instance, "United States fisheries known to Japs" and another, "United States fishermen armed to drive out Japanese." They found that the Japanese were not playing the game; that they were not living up to the agreement with the United States; so these men sent for a couple of hundred rifles and ammunition and they proposed to take the law into their own hands. The situation attracted the attention of the United States government. I do not know whether the minister was aware of it, but I do know that the United States government took the matter up with Japan and I have here the brief they presented. I shall touch on some of the points. They pointed out that beginning in 1930, and ever since then a large number of Japanese fishing fleets, made up of floating canneries and auxiliary vessels, have been operating. The mother ship acts as a floating cannery, or a reduction plant, or a freezing plant as necessity warrants, and they stay through the whole season and take the whole catch back to Japan. The Americans object to that. They say that the reports are becoming more and more insistent and reliable, and during the past season their authenticity has been supported by impressive affidavits and actual photographs of the fishing operations in question.
The Japanese, with their usual diplomacy, explained that they were fishing not for salmon, but for crabs; they said that they were simply engaged in a few exploratory operations, looking for crabs. The white men, however, flew over the mother ship and got

so close to them that they could read the names on the boxes of canned salmon, and they saw thousands of fish on their decks. They could even identify the varieties of fish on the decks of the mother ship and they took photographs. In other words, Japanese diplomacy was rather at a discount. The Americans say that the United States government has understood, from assurances given by the Japanese government, that there are no licenses granted, but that is all a midsummer night's dream. They say they are sorry; but the reports they get and the photographs raise a strong presumption that the Japs actually are fishing there. Then the Americans deal with the enormous trade that they do in Alaskan waters, pointing out that the people of Alaska are allowed to fish only for one month, with the idea of conserving the fish, but the Japanese will fish for the whole period. They say the Japanese fishermen appear to be unrestricted as to season or equipment. Large bodies of United States fishermen are of the opinion that the salmon runs of Bristol bay are a United States resource, as they breed in Alaskan waters. The prospect is that the use of these more effective methods by Japanese nationals, while similar methods are denied to United States fishermen has provoked among United States fishemen serious concern and resentment. It is clear to all that if foreign nationals are permitted to carry on these operations off the shore of Alaska, the conservation efforts of the United States government within a comparatively short period will be of absolutely no effect. They point out that some
25,000	people are employed in the trade in Alaska, what they pay in wages, and the enormous business they do.
Then there is some correspondence. I shall read only a final extract from a confidential release dated March 25, 1938. They say that as a result of discussions between the United States government and the government of Japan in connection with these matters the Japanese government has given, without prejudice of course, assurance as follows: that the Japanese government is suspending- that -means stopping for a short period, doesn't it?-the three year salmon fishing survey which has been in progress since 1936, and inasmuch as salmon fishing by Japanese is not permitted without licence from the Japanese government, that government will continue to suspend the issue of them, and if the United States government will prove Japanese vessels are fishing illegally, they will take cognizance of it. The United States government accepts these assurances and

Supply-Fisheries
hopes they will live up to them. But between the lines you can read considerable doubt about that. Since that, these headings appeared that I have quoted about the United States fishermen arming themselves against the Japanese, because they are still there and are proceeding to fish. It is not a local matter to Alaska, or even British Columbia; it is of nation-wide concern. If that is persisted in, it means that with modern methods they will clean up the whole Pacific coast from Alaska to San Francisco. They can keep offshore, outside territorial waters, and I suppose they are legally correct.
But there are methods of bringing pressure to bear even upon Japan. If it were suggested that there would be retaliation in the way of non-trade, they would probably see reason. But unless the government do something more than tell me I ought to have confidence in the government looking after these matters, I shall not be satisfied. The minister knows the situation; has he taken any steps about it; has he associated himself with the United States in this protest? If not, then if the Japanese make any deal with the United States to keep out of Alaskan waters, there is only one place they will go, namely, to British Columbia waters. Has the minister had any communication with the Japanese or the United States government, so that we might join in any action that has been taken? And it is not only the Japanese; there was a suggestion last year that a British boat was coming from the Atlantic to fish for halibut, also a Norwegian boat. Unless we do something to stop them soon, the Japanese will establish their claim and our fishing will be non est. Will the minister give the committee some information as to what progress has been made in connection with the matter?

As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has stated, this is a delicate matter. These operations are carried on, on the high seas, where the Japanese, Americans, Norwegians, Canadians and others have a legal right to fish. It can be stopped only by mutual agreement between the countries interested, And I * dare say it can be stopped by those countries only by preventing their nationals from resorting to those waters; that is, the Canadian government would have no right or power to prevent natives of a foreign country from carrying on such operations. As stated by my hon. friend, the government of Japan have said that they are going to refuse permits to their own nationals to carry on such operations, and that is the only way by which what is desired can be accomplished. When I said on a
previous occasion that the hon. member should have enough confidence in the government to accept the statement that the matter is in hand and would be looked after, I knew my hon. friend would realize that this was what was intended. As far as the Department of Fisheries is concerned, it is not within our power to take up questions of that kind with foreign countries; all these matters are dealt with through the Department of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. But I know the matter is being dealt with. As far as the Department of Fisheries is empowered, we are following up with a view to protect the sources of supply for our fisheries as much as possible, and trying to impress upon neighbouring countries that the fisheries can be protected for all concerned only by mutual understanding and cooperation in conservation.

No doubt the minister's statements are correct as far as they go, but they are more in the nature of truisms which do not lead to any definite action. He says it can be done only by agreement. I admit that; it is out in the open ocean. And he says that the Japanese government say they have refused to allow their vessels to operate in Alaskan waters. Yes. They promised the United States that, but have they promised us that they will not do it in our waters? We, it must be remembered, are next, and we have under the hand of the Canadian embassy at Washington the assurance that the Americans have been promised that the Japanese will keep out of Alaskan waters; but have we any such assurance? It is just as vital to us as to the Americans, and as far as I can find the fisheries department has done just nothing in the matter. Is that not the situation? If it is not, I shall apologize. If it is not so, will the minister bring down some correspondence showing the progress of negotiations? I submit nothing has been done, but still he asks me to have faith and confidence. Our neighbours to the south have done something; we apparently have done nothing. If we have done anything, what was it? Have we a promise that they will abstain? I have in my hand a long three column page of regulations made by the department in connection with mackerel on the east coast. There are about nine different brands: large, small and medium summer, and dark summer, and large, medium and extra large and choice fall, and dark fall, and so on. I notice that the biggest size in one case is not the biggest in the other; this is calculated to deceive people. It ends by saying that in the event of these sizes not being suitable, the minister may authorize a
Supply-Fisheries

tolerance in the count to suit the requirements of the trade. Is that not a comparatively petty matter? Perhaps $150,000 worth of mackerel is packed, but should not the heads of the department at least be negotiating matters of such vital importance to us on the western coast? If I am wrong, and negotiations have been taking place, what are they? How far have they got? Will the minister bring down the correspondence? If not, will he initiate such correspondence; because it is for us to act to-day, not to-morrow? The Americans made their arrangement on March 25; what have we done?

My hon. friend has read some newspaper clippings intimating that some Japanese boats had been fishing off the coast of Alaska. But he has not shown that any of these boats have been operating in territorial waters along the British Columbia coast, and as far as the department is concerned we do not know of any specific instance of Japanese boats carrying on such operations there. Until we have some specific case to complain about, I do not think we should anticipate any possible operation of that kind in waters adjacent to our country by adopting the methods of negotiation which have been adopted by the United States.

If that is the attitude of the government, I will throw up my hands and not bother them any more. Here is the situation. Suppose there is a war and an enemy fleet lands in Vancouver. Somebody on the prairies says, " It will be time enough for us to fight when they reach Winnipeg." I know they are not doing anything in our waters to-day, but I was trying to look ahead, to galvanize the government into a little foresight in the matter. To-day it is the Alaskan situation, but, the United States have negotiated a treaty-whatever it may be worth-under which the Japanese are to keep out of Alaskan waters. But there is the mother ship and there are these boats; where are they to go next? The minister says it will be time enough to do something when they take some action. It will be too late then, because they will have established a precedent; they will have their equipment ready. Surely it is the part of wisdom to look ahead and try to reach an understanding about these things before they become acute, before there are large sums involved and vested interests concerned.
There is no use saying I quoted newspapers only. I quoted our own Minister to the United States. I obtained this information from Sir Herbert Marler in Washington. This was a confidential intelligence release given

out by the United States government, which finally led up to the announcement that they had successfully-I hope it will be successful in its permanence-negotiated a deal by which the Japanese agreed not to fish outside the territorial waters of Alaska. Is this not the time for us to take some action? But if the minister takes the view that it will be time enough when the enemy is knocking at our door, I am afraid there is no use in discussing the matter.
I should like to ask the minister whether this whole matter does not come within the ambit of the international sockeye commission.
No. Halibut are not sockeye.

In any event I want to say that since the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster I have been rather disconcerted. I understand that this is an international sockeye commission. If the Canadian representative only represents the fishermen of the Fraser river, then I want to ask the minister if he will kindly see that the Canadian representative represents also the district of Nanaimo. I want to feel that the interests of Canada in the matter of salmon are being protected by our representative on the international sockeye commission.
Would the minister tell the hon. member that there are three commissioners, not just one?

Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $240,740.

I think we all regret that almost each year the estimates of this department are brought in on the last day of the session. Under this item I notice that the number of inspectors and those employed in canneries is exactly the same as it was a year ago; thirty-five; there has been no reduction. Seeing that the fish hatcheries in British Columbia have been closed, what portion of this vote will be expended in that province, and for what purpose?

The only expenditure under this head in British Columbia during this fiscal year will be for the payment of the salaries of officers whose leave has not yet expired and who have not been either superannuated or transferred to some other district.

I understand that at the beginning of the present year the control of sport or game fish in non-tidal waters of British Columbia was transferred to the

Criminal Code
province by a federal order in council. That has raised the question of licences. I understand that non-resident anglers' licences are still collected by the federal government, and at present it is understood that the dominion Department of Fisheries have placed licence books in the hands of custom officers and other agents in the interior and along the southern border of the province. One is quite safe in saying that ninety-five per cent of the licences issued will be used in non-tidal waters. This is somewhat confusing, if it has not been straightened out.

I am pleased to be able to inform my hon. friend that we have been able to come to a satisfactory understanding with the government of British Columbia. The federal government has withdrawn from the sport fish business. We have left the field; we do not issue licences any longer, nor do we collect licence fees.
But I understood there was some confusion. We collected a fee for tidal waters and the province collected a non-tidal angler's fee, which meant that the tourist had to pay double.
No; he will not pay any federal fee now.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

He said: The first amendment is to section 12, which deals with the definition of common gaming house. The object of the original amendment to the section was to include within the definition of "common gaming house" one where any direct or indirect fee is charged to or paid by the players or any of them for the right or privilege of participating in a game. There was the exception concerning the house, room or place occasionally being used by a charitable or religious organization for playing a game the proceeds from which are to be used for the benefit of any charitable or religious object.
The senate has added another exception concerning:-

any house, room or place while occupied and used by an incorporated, bona fide social club or branch thereof, if the whole or any portion 51952-284

I understand that unless this amendment had been accepted, the whole section would have been rejected. It is a compromise, and I am quite willing to accept it, although I preferred the section as it was.

The house again in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Special-To enable aiding fishermen, groups of fishermen and others to establish or better establish themselves in the industry, $500,000.

I would ask the minister to place on Hansard the information for which I asked some time ago. Last year parliament voted a sum of money to be distributed among fishermen; it was for a specific purpose. This vote is to enable fishermen, groups of fishermen and others to establish or better establish themselves in the industry. What was done under the vote passed last year? I suppose, in view of the notice given, there will be no difficulty in giving the information.

Last year $500,000 was voted to aid in the reestablishment and reorganization of the dried and pickled fish branches of the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast, which because of world economic conditions had become acutely depressed. It was hoped to rehabilitate those engaged in the industry by granting assistance in processing, storing and marketing, and attempting to expand the demand for the products of the industry by assisting in the provision of

transportation facilities on those portions of the coast where they were inadequate. All of this was to be carried on under conditions to be approved by order in council. Only about $60,000 was expended.
Might we have the details of the expenditures?

A total of $24,451 was expended to increase the demand for fish by way of advertising, mainly in rural newspapers, because it was expected that dried and salt fish would be consumed mainly in rural districts.

Was that all within
Canada?
Yes. About $5,000 was expended to send two men to the West Indies, Puerto Rico, Cuba and other countries in South America, which in the past had taken most of our exports of cured fish.
Who were they?
Mr. O. F. MacKenzie, of Halifax, and Mr. F. Homer Zwicker, of Lunenburg. Mr. MacKenzie received $2,229.70.
How was that amount determined?

That was made up of travelling expenses because he did not accept any remuneration for his time. Mr. Zwicker received $2,717.75 for travelling expenses and a small allowance of $600 or $700 for his time. Both these gentlemen made a report which has been printed and distributed. To the end of the last fiscal year the balance of the vote could not be expended because the propositions made by the department to the industry and by the industry to the department could not be accepted. That is, no mutual understanding could be arrived at as to how this money should be expended, so we decided we had better keep it. However, negotiations are still continuing in the hope of having the industry take care of the weaker sections of the maritimes, such as eastern Nova Scotia and northern New Brunswick. The government is offering to subsidize certain processing plants which are necessary because of loss of European markets and changed conditions. An effort is to be made to get these people to adapt themselves to new methods so that they will be able to process a product which can be marketed more profitably than dried and salt cod.

Some time ago I intended to make a few remarks in connection with the fisheries of the maritime provinces. I shall not impose myself upon the committee

Supply-Fisheries
this evening except to protest to the minister and to his department over the treatment given to the maritime fishermen. Last year $500,000 was voted to rehabilitate the fishermen in the maritime provinces, and the minister now tells us that some $40,000 of that vote was spent in advertising. I consider that the fishermen in the maritime provinces have received very poor treatment from the department, and I take this opportunity to protest to the minister. These facts are well known because the press of these provinces have called attention to the conditions under which the fishermen are living. These men are receiving very little for their fish. As a matter of fact, they have been receiving only starvation prices. This afternoon we listened to hon. members from the west talking about fixing a price of 85 or 874 cents a bushel for wheat. The fishermen of the maritimes have been receiving for their product a price far below what they should. I contend that all the money which was voted last year should be spent along with whatever is being voted this year. The minister must know the conditions that exist, and he must be aware that this money could easily be spent to good advantage in rehabilitating the fishing industry. I shall not weary the committee with any more comments, but I feel that more attention should be paid to this great industry. When money is voted by this parliament for these men I contend that it should be spent by the minister and his department.

I do not think my hon. friend is fully aware of all the facts and circumstances. There were two votes last year, one of $400,000 to assist the needy fishermen, and another vote of $500,000 to rehabilitate the industry. The vote for the needy fishermen has been all expended.
I shall want the particulars of that.

That vote was expended in cooperation with the provinces. My hon. friend must appreciate that these individuals are not the wards of the dominion government. They are not subject to our jurisdiction unless they come within the scope of the fisheries regulations.
Many .individuals in other industries in Canada have become the wards of the government.

Unfortunately. The Department of Fisheries has recognized its obligations in this emergency. This is the primary responsibility of the provinces, but 51952-2844
the federal government has offered to cooperate in helping the needy fishermen. Agreements have been signed with Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and also Quebec in connection with that portion of the province still under federal jurisdiction, that is, the Magdalen islands.
We have entered into successful agreements whereby we have allowed to Nova Scotia $150,000; to New Brunswick, $100,000; to Prince Edward Island, $50,000, and to Quebec, $50,000. We have kept in reserve a certain amount which was offered to another province and which was declined because conditions there were not such that they could embark upon the policy which was suggested by us. So, as far as the money voted for the individual fisherman is concerned, I think we have done our duty by appropriating it to the provinces in proportion to the number of fishermen registered in each of such provinces.
Again this year we are negotiating with the same provinces with a view of continuing the help -which was given for the last two years. As far as individuals are concerned we are leaving it with the provinces to determine what methods should be adopted to help them. Even in one province the problem is not the same in all sections, and it would be very difficult to adopt in Ottawa a uniform policy applicable even to one province. We prefer leaving this to the provincial governments that are willing to cooperate with us.
As to the industry, we are trying to adopt the best methods possible to help it and place it in a position where those engaged in it can regain the standard which they held prior to the depression. I am pleased to state that in this year we have reached a point where the fishing industry is back to where it was in 1930.

With regard to the
amounts allotted to the provinces, have the provinces taken advantage of those allotments? I have here a return which I received some time ago from the department indicating the contributions to provincial funds from which aid was given by the provinces concerned in establishing or better establishing groups of fishermen in the industry. I notice from the return that Nova Scotia expended $96,792.99; Prince Edward Island, $42,406, and New Brunswick, only $1S,180. I should like to know why so small an amount was expended in New Brunswick, and why it W'as expended only in one month out of the twelve months? Nova Scotia seems

to have taken advantage of it for eleven months of the year, and Prince Edward Island, for eight months.

This was due to the
fact that at the time that information was given to the hon. member, accounts for these amounts only had been rendered to us. Since then, further accounts have been rendered, and up to the time that these estimates were made Nova Scotia had paid out $100,000; New Brunswick, $75,000; Prince Edward Island, $77,000, and Quebec, $75,000.
How about British Columbia?

They did not expend
anything.

Will any portion of this
sum be made available to aid the fishermen of British Columbia? If no agreement exists, is there any prospect of an agreement with British Columbia ?

A portion of it was
offered to that province, but no agreement was entered into. The prospects of entering into an agreement depend on the attitude of the province.

The minister knows that I have taken a deep interest in this matter, for reasons which, I think, are obvious to every thoughtful man. Nova Scotia is a pretty rocky province. In pre-glacial days there was some soil on the rocks, but the soil has been largely removed, and these people live on a very rocky coast. I have visited their communities. I learn from the press that they are getting one cent and one and a half cents a pound for halibut, and the consumer is paying anywhere from twenty to twenty-five cents. As the minister knows, cod brings a much smaller price. These are facts. It is true that the amount I mention is an extremely depressed price. We know what the Atlantic halibut is, compared with the Pacific halibut; it is a smaller fish. They have also the haddock, which is an excellent fish, and the cod, which is not as clean as the others. These fish are being sold to-day at a very low price by the fishermen. When I say

they are getting a cent and a cent and a half per pound, and the fillets are being sold on the markets to consumers at fifteen cents and as high as twenty-five cents a pound, the minister will realize what the condition of mind of these fishermen is. Certainly- it is an attitude of great resentment against conditions. Everyone knows that.
I have a suggestion to make to the minister. Last year we voted a large sum of money to help the industry. To-day the minister has given an explanation of why only $60,000 has been spent. We now come to the other half million dollars which has to do with the individual fisherman, and what do we find? We find that in one of the provinces we gave $150,000 under the terms of an agreement by which we exercise little or no jurisdiction over the spending of it, leaving it, for the reasons the minister mentioned, to the province to deal with. In New Brunswick the situation is the same. I have followed with increasing interest the operations of the cooperative movement in Nova Scotia. Whatever else may be said, Mr. MacDonald, who is associated with St. Francis Xavier university, has done a most remarkable work. They endeavoured to get him to go to upper Canada. Fortunately Nova Scotia has retained his services. When he was here the other day I had an opportunity to talk with him regarding the work which is being done in Nova Scotia. I suggest to the minister that he should make available out of this sum of money a substantial grant to assist in cooperative enterprises among these fishermen. I believe that by so doing he will achieve a very great reform, and of course he is anxious to do so.
And, sir, I know something more. I know of the money that is being made out of the fishing industry. I recall a man who left Halifax with a reasonably small sum of money; he went down to a Nova Scotian port and established a fishing industry, and in combination with a great company which has existed in that industry he has made a substantial fortune. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth^Clare probably knows whom I mean, although I am not mentioning any name. He acquired a very large sum, somewhere, I believe, between a quarter and half a million dollars. To no small extent that fortune should have been distributed under proper conditions amongst the fishermen themselves, because the inability to sell their fish for more than one or one and a half cents per pound made possible the accumulation of these large returns. I suggest that the minister utilize some part of

Supply-Fisheries
this vote-and he will have everybody behind him in doing so-in helping these poor unfortunate men to forward a cooperative movement which will ensure that a larger part of the price paid by the consumer goes into their pockets.

Members of the committee must have noticed in the main estimates that we have this year for the first time an appropriation-small indeed- to the United Maritime Fisheries organization, which is the central organization of the cooperatives of Nova Scotia.
Yes, but it is only $3,000.
That is for organization purposes.
What good is that?

Besides this, we have an agreement, under another head, with the extension department of St. Francis Xavier university whereby we vote them an appropriation to cover the expenses of carrying on their movement in the three maritime provinces.
How much is that?
Eight thousand dollars this year.
Quite. Well, they spend $25,000 per annum.

I know. But this movement is growing and we are increasing our grant each year. We are in constant consultation with the head of the department, Doctor Coady, under whom Doctor MacDonald works, and we follow exactly their directions. We leave them free to act as they feel they should. I may take the committee into my confidence and say that last year we were willing to put a substantial amount at the disposal of the organization to help them to establish a base on the eastern coast of Nova Scotia, but as will be seen from their petition and the records of the department they were not yet prepared to take advantage of the offer and were not sufficiently well organized to begin in a large way to take care of themselves. That is one of the main reasons why the amount was not given them. Admittedly they were not ready to take advantage of the offer. They wanted the government to start a publicly owned plant, and the opinion was shared by the heads of the movement that this was not the proper thing to do. It was felt that we had better wait a little while until these people were ready to take hold of the movement themselves and to administer their own business without any governmental interference or control.
The minister will admit that a cent or a half-cent a pound is ruinous.

Absolutely, and if we knew of any method whereby we could compel those through whom the fish is processed and marketed to pay higher prices, it would be done. The only hope is to encourage these cooperative movements so as to enable them to manage their own affairs and market the products of their own industry in order that they may get everything that is in it and enjoy all the profits.
Try icing a few cars and paying the freight on them from the seaboard to upper Canada.

speechtext: That was done a few years ago.
Yes, but it was stopped before it was developed.

The trouble arises in connection with the distribution. The organization is not quite prepared to take care of distribution in foreign markets, and until they are ready to do so, I do not think it would be in their own interests-they say so themselves -to go ahead too fast and to undertake a venture which might bring ruin to themselves and discredit upon the organization.

While the amount of $2,000 given for organization purposes may do some good, we cannot obtain lasting benefit unless we give a sufficient amount of money to the cooperative societies. A good many people, no doubt, share my conviction in this regard, but the idea may prevail that this is a partisan or a religious movement, merely because it is sponsored by St. Francis Xavier university. I can assure the committee, however, that the cooperative movement in Nova Scotia is non-sectarian and non-political. I had the pleasure of listening to the Rev. Nelson MacDonald when he explained the aims and objects of the society. I fancy he is known to most members here, by reputation at least, because he is one of the most assiduous workers in the cause of the cooperative movement, working hand in hand with the St. Francis Xavier extension movement. If we want any lasting benefit, I repeat, we must give the greater proportion of the money to some extension movement to educate the fishermen. You may spend all the money you like, but unless you spend money to educate the fishermen you will not get any permanent results. Give them a course of six months or a year under such leadership as is provided by the extension movement to which I have referred. In other parts of the country other
Supply-Fisheries

colleges may come into the picture; perhaps they may be in a better position by reason of location to further the work. At the present time, however, we have only the St. Francis Xavier extension movement in eastern Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and if you gave them $100,000 you would get more value for the money and it would result in more ultimate good for the fishermen than from other expenditures. The cooperative movement is not local; it has assumed international proportions, and the day has gone when you can regard it as purely local.
I am not going to take sides and argue whether the trawlers should or should not operate. As a matter of fact, I do not believe there is anyone in Canada to-day who can argue convincingly on that question, and therefore I suggest that we should move cautiously before making any change in our system in that respect. I do urge, however, that if you give the fishermen proper leadership and the educational facilities furnished by the extension society, you will enable them to look after themselves. One of the chief things they are taught is to look after their financial condition and the processing of their fish. I hold that through the processing of the fish the market in the future will be gained, and the benefit that will accrue to the fishermen will depend upon their ability to process fish in such a way as to render them salable to the rest of the country.
I know that the great concerns which have operated in the past, the fish companies, deserve some credit; in fact they deserve a good deal of credit. For one thing, we cannot overlook the fact that they established the market; they placed their fish on the markets of the rvorld. You cannot, therefore, eliminate these great fish concerns and expect the fishermen to step in at once and fill the gap. I do urge, however, that they be given an amount of money which would enable the St. Francis Xavier organization, or any other college that wishes to take up the work, to function. I am speaking irrespective of any religious denomination or political persuasion. If this were done, the fishermen would be able to look after themselves and to process their fish properly, and they would be ready to fill the gap that would be left by the elimination of the large fish companies if that were necessary

and it will be observed that I add that proviso. It may not be necessary. My guess is as good as anybody else's, I suggest that we are going through a transition period in the economical distribution of foods of all kinds, and there is no man, I do not care how good an economist he may be, or how many letters he may have after his name, who can 
tell the people what the outcome is likely to be so far as distribution is concerned. The minister will have the whole-hearted endorsa-tion of the country if he devotes a greater amount of money to the cause I have been advocating. Do not give it away, as in the past, to ship-owners, but give it to a worthy extension movement which will put the fishermen on a higher plane and enable them to look after their own interests. That would be doing something worthy of the government of Canada.

I realize that the time
is late, but we have waited five months for the fisheries estimates, and this is our first opportunity. I would impress upon the minister that there has been developing in the maritime provinces a condition which is serious in two ways. It is serious from the standpoint of the individual and from the standpoint of the industry. The individual is getting to the point where he is becoming discouraged, and in any project which we undertake we must realize that the individual himself must be convinced that the department is willing to assist him in his difficulties. It is not sufficient to- think only of the industry; we must attack the problem fundamentally from the standpoint of the individual. Until we convince the fisherman that we are willing and anxious to help him and are in with him in this fight, we shall not get very far with broad policies touching the industry only. I suggest to the minister that tt'hen he distributes this amount he think of having the dominion government, the provincial government and the individual fishermen acting in cooperation. All three must come in before any lasting good to the fishermen or the industry is achieved. At this late stage of the session it is impossible to deal with the matter at greater length, but I ask with final emphasis that the minister think particularly of the help he can give to the individual fisherman to encourage him and restore his enthusiasm.
Item agreed to.
Mines and geology branch-Payment in connection with the movement of coal under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, $2,250,000.

Here is an item of
great importance, a couple of million dollars or more. It involves a national policy with respect to fuel. It affects largely the mari-times, and to some small extent western Canada. The movement of coal from the east to the more densely settled communities

Supply-Mines and Geology
has been going forward slowly, but the realization of our expectation of a million more tons of coal being lifted in Cape Breton than formerly as a result of this policy, is now an accomplished fact. But I have been reading with a good deal of care something that touches this matter. There are in Nova Scotia two great enterprises-or were; I do not know whether you can now call them two or not-the Dominion Steel Company, and for the purpose of this statement we will call it the Nova Scotia Steel Company; among the companies it owned was a coal companj' called the Acadia Coal Company.
I observed the other day that there has been some discussion with respect to this matter in connection with its liquidation, and I made up my mind that I would bring it to the attention of the minister. If we are to have a stock-jobbing proposition with respect to this company; that is, if the Acadia company is to be acquired by Scotia and then Scotia is to be closed down and Acadia closed down and the Dominion company issue shares or securities or guarantee payments in any sense, the time has come when we must make it perfectly clear that if there is a curtailment of subsidies because money is used for those purposes, that should be utilized for the purposes for which we voted it, then the complaints that will come should be complaints made to those responsible for this action being taken, and not against this parliament. This parliament has provided money for these purposes, but is not providing money for stock-jobbing exploitations. That is what I want to bring home to the minister.
If anything such as the newspapers indicate is contemplated, he should make it his business now to ascertain what is being done and prevent it from being done out of moneys provided by the taxpayers of Canada in connection with the movement of coal from Cape Breton and other parts of Nova Scotia to the more central parts of this country. It has been a difficult matter to educate the people of the central regions of this country to purchase their coal requirements from the maritimes. It has been an effort on the part of governments, not of one party but of all parties, to get them to take that point of view. It is fundamental that the great enterprise in Cape Breton should not be utilized for stock-jobbing exploitation by the use of any part of the moneys which we pay in large sums-large sums, mark you!-to assist in employment on that island. This money should not be Used to advance the interests and stockjobbing ambitions of those who have been responsible for some of the happenings which
are now before the courts of this country. I give the minister timely warning in order that he may take steps to see that the government is protected by appropriate action, and by doing so he will prevent what I regard as a very serious matter and ensure that these subsidies, heavy as they are, are utilized for the purpose of providing for employment and the development of a fuel policy that will enable this coal from Nova Scotia to be utilized as it now is in the consuming markets of upper Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
My right hon. friend's statement is the first I have heard of the matter.
I understand two of the companies mentioned are in financial difficulty or liquidation. I quite agree with the general principle he has enunciated. Certainly I would be the last one in this house to support the payment of public moneys for stock-jobbing propositions of any kind.
I believe that; that is the reason I bring the matter up here.
I shall be glad to get some information in regard to what my right hon. friend has said.
How much of this money was expended for the movement of coal from the coal areas of New Brunswick last year?
It amounted to $32,362.

The amount paid in New Brunswick is not at all in proportion to the amount paid in Nova Scotia. If we received the same proportion in New Brunswick, I think we would get about ten times that much, or about $300,000. Would the minister look into this matter and see that the coal areas of New Brunswick receive the same consideration that is given the coal areas of Nova Scotia?

Nova Scotia is in a preferred position because a large amount of its coal moves by water. It is my information that even in New Brunswick the mines have not anything like succeeded in supplying the requirements of that province.
The difficulty is that the assistance given under this vote is enabling Nova Scotia to displace New Brunswick coal even in that province.

The fact of the matter is that the basis upon which the subventions are paid apply precisely the same in New Brunswick as they do in Nova Scotia. If a variation should be made to meet the suggestion
Supply-Mines and Geology

of my hon. friend, it would simply mean tha; New Brunswick would be getting something over and above what Nova Scotia was getting. I shall leave it to the imagination of my hon. friend and of the committee as to what would happen under those circumstances.

Has the minister given any consideration to the possibility of stabilizing these subventions? At the present time they are voted by parliament year by year, and we in western Canada think it would help the industry if this was done by statute for a period of five or seven years. Then the subventions would be sufficiently stable for mining interests to invest in mines and establish warehouses in Ontario in order to compete for the markets now supplied by United States coal. I wonder if that policy has been considered at all.

No. I should be glad to
give consideration to it, but I would point out to my hon. friend that since we have had these subventions they have been applied on the same basis. Without having given the question a great deal of thought, I should say that very careful consideration should be given before making any change. However, I shall be glad to keep in mind the suggestion of my hon. friend.
The minister will find in the files of the department that the suggestion has been advanced.

I have just a few words to say about these subventions and about conditions in the coal mining areas of the country. Some hon. members were asking whether or not consideration has been given to the equalization of rates in order to get down to a stable basis. As I see it, the chief trouble in Canada is that we have not given the coal situation, with regard to Nova Scotia or any other province, enough consideration to know really what it is all about. I do not attribute this situation to the minister at all; but he is supposed to be aided by the fuel board, and I venture to suggest that this board has not met as such for a couple of years. I may be wrong, but I very much doubt if it has. Of course I know that the secretary is indefatigable in his efforts, but I doubt if the board has ever had a real meeting. It exists in name only, and what is the result?
I wish I had more time at my disposal to deal with this question, but I do not want to block this item at all. However, I think this is the opportune time to say what I have in mind, and I believe I should be doing wrong if I did not bring to the attention of the

minister a few suggestions which I consider may be helpful. The first is that in spite of slack employment conditions in the coal mines of Nova Scotia I venture the prediction that there has been no slackening in the importation of coal into central Canada. There would be no need for only three or four days work a week in the coal mines of Cape Breton or any other part of Canada if we did not import so much bituminous coal from the United States. According to my information that importation amounted to 9,720,000 tons last year. I do not want to enlarge on that; I think hon. members can get the point as well from those few words as if I spoke for an hour or two.
I go now to another matter to which not only the fuel board but also the minister should give some attention. While we do not stand in the way of progress; while we realize that progressive methods must be introduced in industry in order to increase efficiency, still industry owes something to this government as representing the people of Canada. This, I think, is a most inopportune time for any company to install electrical devices which will automatically throw one-third of the working population out of employment. That is just about what we are facing in Cape Breton to-day. I do not wish to obstruct progress; I believe in progress, and I realize that the time is coming when electrical mechanization will be the only process used in mining coal. But at this time, when unemployment is such a great issue in this country,
I say these people should be slowed down. Let them introduce it to some extent; let them try it out if they wish, but I think the introduction of electrical mechanization into the coal mines of Nova Scotia gives the explanation to the problem presented by the right hon. leader of the opposition in his reference to the Acadia coal area. Take one electrical unit in a mine. It will produce perhaps 250 tons of coal, and will require perhaps eleven men. Put ten units in a mine, and you will have 2,500 tons of coal spilling out of that mine if these machines work efficiently, as I believe they do. With eleven men to a unit that would mean 110 men. Then put three men, let us say, behind every man attached to the unit. There you have a small crew producing 2,500 tons of coal a day. It is easy to figure out the result; it does not require any advanced mathematics. If you electrify three or four mines, you will drop about a third of your crews; instead of having 1,800 men at work, you will employ only 600 or 800 men at the most. The remainder

Supply-Mines and Geology
will be a burden on the people of this country, and ultimately a large part of the coal mining districts will close down.
My argument is that while neither I nor any other member of this house would want to obstruct progress, this electrification process should go forward very slowly, so as to not throw into the ranks of the unemployed a large number of men whom the rest of the people will have to support, making so much worse the unemployment situation of the country. These are faots which cannot be gainsaid. I do not make the statement critically, but I doubt very much whether the government as a whole is cognizant of what is happening throughout the dominion. I again come back to the fishermen and point out that we are in a transitional stage. By ignoring the fact that we are in a transitional stage we shall not improve our unemployment situation. Rather than throw back on to the unemployment lists a great number of men, let us increase the coal subventions by giving a higher rate, or even by an amount of money equivalent to that which would otherwise have to be paid to the unemployed, if they were pushed on to relief.
I think the economic outlook the government should take would be that of considering the man power, the greatest economic factor in Canada. If the government does not look at what is happening, with the men working only two or three days a week in Nova Scotia, and coal still being imported in the vast quantities I have mentioned, we shall have another 9,000,000 or 10,000,000 tons of bituminous coal coming into Canada.
A short time ago the hon. member for Royal spoke about New Brunswick. In that connection, if the government had been on the alert, and had been watching what was happening, the condition of affairs he described would never have been allowed to exist. The royal commission appointed to investigate conditions brought out the facts that the conditions under which those people are living are horrible in the extreme. What was happening at the same time? At the same time our government owned railways were playing the coal miners of New Brunswick against the coal miners of Nova Scotia, to keep the price down. They got their coal from New Brunswick for from $3.20 to $3.60 per ton. Is that taking into consideration the economic man power of Canada? I submit it is not. These are factors which should be gone into exhaustively by a fuel board, so that they may know what is happening in our coal industry.
We do not know what the future of coal mining may be. I do not pretend to know. But I say that during this transitional period the lot of the coal miner in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta and British Columbia can be eased a great deal by having correct supervision by a board which would take an active interest. I bring these facts to the attention of the committee, not by way of criticism, but in the hope that the minister may take action to see that the conditions are investigated, and that they will not continue to exist. I trust that he will see to it that conditions do not become much worse than they are at the present time. If those men are thrown out of work, our unemployment situation will become aggravated to a great extent.
Some of us regret that the item has not been brought down until this late hour.
Carried.

No; it is not carried yet. There are some of us who refrained from debating the budget because we believed we would have the privilege of talking on this item, and saying what we wanted to say. However, we find that now we are almost within minutes of the time for prorogation. I protest against that procedure. Under the circumstances I shall limit myself to saying briefly what I want to say. The hon. member who has just spoken has brought to the attention of the government the matter as it relates to the unemployment situation in Canada. Last year this situation was placed before the national employment commission, and Mr. Purvis delegated a special man'so far as possible to investigate whether or not if operating at capacity, the coal mining industry could relieve the unemployment situation in this country. We understood something would be done in the present year. We now notice that the commission's report has been presented, and the matter entirely ignored. I cannot emphasize too much the fact that if the coal situation were viewed from a national standpoint, we would to a very great extent solve our unemployment problem.
We should have time to go into a discussion of the matter from a national point of view. The coal mining industry of Canada is almost on its last legs, if the matter is not dealt with within a very short space of time. I should like to know how much of the appropriation goes to the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia and how much to Alberta?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had hoped it would be possible to announce prorogation this evening. There are, however, still a number of items which have to be passed, and it might be pressing the house unduly were we to seek to pass all the votes to-night. There are not very many, but it might be thought a bit arbitrary on the part of the government were I to urge hon. members to remain until all were passed. Possibly, therefore, the suggestion of the former Minister of Public Works, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), might be accepted, and the house adjourn at the present time. I believe hon. members generally are anxious to have prorogation as soon as possible, and were we to meet a little earlier to-morrow morning, we might definitely decide to arrange for prorogation at one o'clock. The government is always in the hands of the house in seeking to make an arrangement of the kind, and no one can say exactly what hour can be fixed, but I believe that we should be able to count on prorogation by one o'clock to-morrow were we to adjourn now and reassemble at 10.30 o'clock in the morning.

Penitentiaries Commission Act
I wish to say a word about prorogation itself. As hon. members are aware, His Excellency the Governor General has arranged to pay a visit to England this summer. About three months ago, in conversation with His Excellency, I suggested, that, having regard to the probable length of the session, it might be well not to fix a time for sailing before the first week of July and His Excellency so arranged. For some weeks past his sailing has been fixed for July 1st which is to-morrow. He is here this evening. As hon. members are aware His Excellency has been in residence at the Citadel in Quebec city for the past few weeks. He left Quebec this morning in anticipation of prorogation of parliament this evening. He is quite prepared to prorogue parliament at three or four in the morning. Moreover, His Excellency is quite prepared to postpone his sailing another week should his not being present to prorogue parliament occasion any disappointment. I feel that I will have the support of the house if I advise His Excellency not to alter, at this late time, his plans for sailing but to leave from Quebec to-morrow on his journey across the sea. I intend to advise him accordingly and shall arrange for prorogation by the deputy of the governor general. That is all I wish to say in that respect. If it is the wish of the house that we do not sit later to-night, the committee might rise now and report progress and ask leave to sit again, and after that is done I shall have a motion to propose, that for its next sitting the house meet at halfpast ten o'clock in the morning.
Ten o'clock.
Carry on.

That can be done only with unanimous consent. This is another day and I object to continuing after midnight. I shall be glad to meet the wishes of the Prime Minister and agree to the house meeting at 10.30 o'clock.
Progress reported.
